Guides to SQL databases in RustStream services with ruststream-sqlx: task queues in the service's tables and a transactional outbox.
How a queue in a SQL table works, where ruststream-sqlx sits between the database and the RustStream runtime, and what that costs.
What ruststream-sqlx costs on every message: throughput against a raw sqlx loop, the outbox as a plugin, and the instructions and allocations of its code.
How ruststream-sqlx measures itself: the three loops, the run on a real database, the database-bound arithmetic, the throughput grid and the code count.
What the benchmark numbers of ruststream-sqlx measure, what still costs a message, and what the numbers do not allow you to conclude.
Where ruststream-sqlx sits: between the RustStream runtime and the service's sqlx pool, with SQL built once per subscription and the outbox beside any broker.
One subscription keeps a claim in flight per free worker, within the pool's size less one; workers_by_key(n) keeps each partition key on one lane.
The constructor records configuration, connect builds the pool and picks the dialect, a subscription prepares its SQL at startup, and shutdown stops the claims.
The outbox records each publish in a table of the service's own, on any broker, marks the record once a consumer acknowledges, and resends the rest at startup.
The way of a row through a service: claim, delivery, decode, handler, reply and settlement, one row at a time, in batches, or as the row itself.
A queue is a table of the service's own: a row is a message, a group is a queue, and the roles of the columns decide when a row is due and what an outcome does.
Three ways to claim a row: a row lock held by an open transaction, a lease written into the row, and an advisory lock on a key, each priced in connections.
The transactions the crate opens for a delivery: the row lock form's claim, and in transactional mode the one a handler writes through, at the table's level.
A subscription claims while its claims come back full, and otherwise waits its poll interval, which a publish of the same broker or a notification cuts short.
What ack, drop, retry and retry_after write into a queue table in each claim form, and how the attempt count and the dead letter turn a retry into a move.
ruststream-sqlx serves task queues in the service's own SQL tables and tracks what a service publishes on any broker in an outbox.
With asyncapi the document names the database server and, on each subscription's channel, the table it reads and its group; rows get their schema.
Each InboxQueue channel carries x-ruststream-sqlx: the table it reads, qualified with its schema, and the group its name selects where the table has groups.
The server is the pool's host and port with the protocol postgres or mysql, SQLite in process with no host, an AnyPool by its scheme, never a credential.
SqlxBroker serves queues from the service's tables through a sqlx pool, built at connect or the service's own; connect checks a connection and picks a dialect.
Each message in work holds pool connections by its form; workers(n) claims in parallel but always leaves the pool one connection for handlers.
SqlxBrokerError is the inbox's one error type: connecting, statements, the schema, declarations, leases, transactions, publishes, and a closed broker.
One glob, ruststream_sqlx::prelude, brings the core prelude, the derives, the broker, InboxQueue, its steps, the publish policies and the keys.
Shutdown returns ClosedSqlxBroker, releases every advisory lock in work, and a publisher kept past it reports SqlxBrokerError::Closed.
A subscription builds and prepares its statements when it opens, so a missing table or column, a retry the table cannot carry or a second reader stops startup.
A handler reads the inbox's context through Ctx<keys::..>: the transaction, the pool and the attempt, in that order, leaving out what it does not need.
keys::Attempt reads the delivery's attempt, 1 for the first: the attempt column as it stood before the claim, None where the table has none.
keys::Pool gives a handler the service's pool, whose writes commit on their own whatever the outcome; on dedicated threads it is the thread's pool.
SqlxBroker takes the dialect built in for its database; statements are built once when a subscription opens, the insert at compile time.
With any, an AnyPool is served by the built-in dialect of the database it reaches at connect; its rows hold integers, text and bytes only.
SqlxBroker::with_dialect serves a database with a dialect of the service's own: Dialect, then the trait of each form it builds, and ByName for names.
mysql serves MySQL 8.0.1 and MariaDB 10.6 or later in every form, READ COMMITTED by default; index the claim order so a claim reads its own group.
On Postgres every form runs: SKIP LOCKED claims, a one-statement lease claim, advisory locks on 64-bit hashes, statement_timestamp and LISTEN/NOTIFY.
sqlite serves the lease and advisory lock forms in the service's process: one writer at a time, times as text, and no server to run in tests.
A table takes rows by row lock unless it names another form: FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED in a transaction held while the handler runs.
advisory_lock = ".." holds each row by a lock on its key: rows that share a key go into work one at a time, and a crashed session frees its rows.
#[field(locked_until)] selects the lease form: the claim writes an expiry and commits, the handler holds no connection, and the lease is extended.
custom(lock, unlock) hands the lock and the release of each key to the service's SQL, so a queue shares a lock another system already takes.
A headers column keeps a delivery's headers as a JSON object of strings; a publish with a header the column cannot hold is refused.
custom(fetch) reads the claimed rows with the service's own SELECT, such as a join; a claimed id it returns no row for settles by the decode policy.
HeaderColumn lets a headers column hold a type of the service's own; it moves the map in and out and names a header it cannot keep byte for byte.
Each field of a headers struct without a role is a header: strings and bytes as they are, numbers in decimal, times in RFC 3339, None left out.
In the headers layout a headers struct describes the queue table and its header fields, and the message struct that flattens it is what a handler takes.
A table with a payload column is in payload mode: the claim lends the column's bytes to the codec, and the handler takes the decoded message.
A claimed row that does not decode is settled by the subscription's decode policy before the handler runs, and still spends its attempt.
A table without a payload column is in row mode: a handler takes the struct itself as the driver read it, one row or a slice per claim.
The outbox records each message a service publishes under a registered name until a consumer processed it, and publishes the rest again at startup.
The outbox wraps inbox handlers as any other; a record written from a transactional handler commits on its own, whatever the delivery's outcome.
OutboxError names what the outbox could not do: record, read or republish a publish, publish with no pool, or write past a SQLite write lock.
#[derive(Outbox)] describes the outbox table: id, name and payload are required, headers and processed_at optional; the service writes the record.
outbox! registers record types under the names they track and returns the registry; a name written twice does not compile.
b.after_startup(policy, tracking.republish()) sends every unprocessed record again once the subscriptions are open; republish_names picks names.
Inside #[ruststream::app] the registry starts without a pool, and on_startup builds one and hands it over with set_pool; the service closes it.
custom(fetch, ack, retry, discard, recover) replaces a record's default statement with the service's own, for a status of its own or a saga.
A test build leaves the outbox off, so a test needs no outbox table; RUSTSTREAM_SQLX_OUTBOX=on turns it on for the whole test process.
Outbox::layer and publish_layer track messages: the publish records then sends, and the delivery's outcome settles its record by its id.
Outbox::wrap gives a publisher outside the publish pipeline the same tracking, for an HTTP endpoint or an after_startup hook.
A publish writes a row through the row's Publish, the service's own INSERT; Repository names the table at compile time, a static call per publish.
SqlxBroker::route leads a name into a row type's table in both directions; Routed, the default for replies and slots, looks each name up.
A handler's outcome is a statement on its row: ack deletes it or sets processed_at, retry returns it at once with one more attempt, drop finishes it.
max_attempts(n) with dead_letter(..) moves a row whose attempts are spent into another group, or into a table with the same columns.
retry_after(d) hides the row until its retry_after column comes due; a table without the column returns the row at once and logs a warning.
InboxQueue reads one queue of a table: its name selects a group where the table has a group column and addresses the whole table where it has none.
A slice handler gets one claim of up to batch(n) rows; each row settles on its own, and in the row lock form the settlements commit together.
#[field(group, fifo = true)] keeps each group in order: one row of a group in work at a time across every broker, the head first.
A subscription by name, #[subscriber("emails")], reads the table its route leads to; it takes the broker's settings and no retry cap.
on_threads runs an InboxQueue subscription's handlers on dedicated threads, each with a pool of its own, counted against connection_limit.
A subscription claims while its claims come back full, then waits the poll interval, one second unless the broker or the queue sets another.
workers(n) keeps a claim in flight for each free worker, bounded by the pool; with a partition_key column workers_by_key(n) keeps each key in order.
#[derive(Inbox)] describes a queue table with an ordinary sqlx struct: the table in #[inbox(..)], column roles in #[field(..)], names from sqlx.
#[inbox(checked, db = ..)] puts the statements a struct determines into sqlx's compile-time check against DATABASE_URL or the .sqlx offline data.
A column is named in one place, sqlx's attributes: rename, rename_all, raw identifiers and skip; a flattened field makes statements select every column.
custom(..) hands one event of a table to the service's own SQL, Claim to Extend, and every other event keeps the statement the dialect builds.
A table described by hand implements InboxTable: a const InboxSpec chain, its settings as types in type Table, and the same statements as the derive.
Insert writes a task with the derive's generated insert, inside the service's own transaction, so the task commits with the data it serves.
Each #[field(..)] role turns on one behaviour of the queue: group, priority, partition key, retry_after, attempt, processed_at, lease, headers, payload.
TestApp::start runs the service against a real database, SQLite in memory for a start, with the harness waiting on every publish and a pausable clock.
TestApp::start_live runs the same test body on the real clock, against a database of the test's own on Postgres, MySQL or MariaDB.
A queue reads "now" to claim, delay and mark rows; by default the host's SystemClock, bound in the column's own type as the service's inserts do.
A clock of the service's own implements Clock and takes the place of SystemClock in clock = .. or .clock::<..>(), for every statement that reads now.
clock = DatabaseClock makes the statements read the database's clock, so every host serving one table reads one clock; the lease form keeps the host's.
A time column holds chrono::DateTime<Utc> or time::OffsetDateTime; SQLite compares times as text, exact for chrono and to the second for time.
.transactional() lends the handler its delivery's transaction: acknowledgement commits the handler's writes with the row's settlement, or neither.
isolation = <level> opens a table's transactions at an isolation level, mode = <mode> at a SQLite mode; a level the dialect does not open does not compile.
A publish through the broker wakes the subscriptions of its table and group in the same process at once; a row written by other means waits the poll.
On Postgres, listen_notify wakes subscriptions on pg_notify from any process: each publish announces its row, and a trigger can announce others.

documents.t: ruststream-sqlx brings SQL databases into a RustStream service through sqlx. It has two parts. The inbox is a task queue in the service's own table, served as a RustStream broker. The outbox records what a service publishes on any RustStream broker until a consumer has processed it. Both run on Postgres, MySQL and MariaDB, and SQLite. The guides take a service from a first queue on SQLite through retries, ordering, transactions and several instances to production on Postgres, and track what it publishes on other brokers. Start with Getting started.
This section draws how a queue in a SQL table works, where ruststream-sqlx sits between the database and the RustStream runtime, and what that costs a service.
What ruststream-sqlx costs on every message: throughput against a raw sqlx loop, the outbox as a plugin, and the instructions and allocations of its code.

The first chart runs each scenario three ways on the stand's PostgreSQL. Raw sqlx loop is a loop written by hand that runs the statements the broker runs for the same table, in the same order, on a pool built the same way; it takes them from the dialect, so the two cannot drift apart. Crate by hand drives this crate's subscription or publisher with a loop of its own and no runtime. RustStream service is the service a user writes: a #[derive(Inbox)] table, a #[subscriber] handler and the app. The first gap is what this crate costs over the statements it runs, and the second is what the runtime adds on top. Each loop is a bar from its best round to its slowest, with a dot at the best round and a notch at the median. The zero of the axis is the raw loop's best round, and a dot right of zero is slower. A hollow dot is a loop whose difference from the raw loop is smaller than the spread of the rounds. The table under the chart prints the best round with the median in parentheses. Every message costs at least a claim, a settlement and a commit, each a round trip to the database. A row marked database-bound is one whose raw loop spent at least half of each message waiting on those round trips. The crate and the runtime then do their work inside a wait the raw loop pays as well, and the row is a lower bound on their cost rather than a measurement of it.

The outbox works over any broker, so it is measured as a cost to an ordinary app: one app in three variants, over the stand's Redis Pub/Sub through ruststream-fred and the stand's PostgreSQL. Without the outbox is the app a user writes without one. Outbox written by hand is the same app with the record inserted before each publish, then fetched and marked in the handler, in raw sqlx. The crate's outbox is the same app with this crate's registry, its two layers and the republish. Against no outbox the chart shows what tracking a message costs at all; against the outbox by hand it shows what the crate's machinery adds to the statements a user would run anyway.

The cost chart counts what one message costs on the service's thread: instructions under callgrind and allocations under DHAT, in the steady state, against the stand's PostgreSQL. The count holds the runtime, this crate and sqlx's driver encoding and decoding on that thread; the database server is another process and is not counted. Cold start is what starting the service costs once: opening the pool's connections, the broker's startup checks and the first delivery. The outbox's counts run the same apps over MemoryBroker, so no transport is in their number.

How ruststream-sqlx measures itself: the three loops, the run on a real database, the database-bound arithmetic, the throughput grid and the code count. The procedure is the framework's own (RustStream methodology), and this page states what it is on a SQL database.

One process runs each scenario three times over, as three loops that differ in one thing: what carries the messages. Raw sqlx loop. sqlx, driven directly: a loop that runs the statements the broker runs for the same table, in the same order, on a pool built the same way. It takes its statements from the dialect the broker renders them with, so the two loops run the same SQL. Crate by hand. This crate and nothing above it: the broker connects, an InboxQueue opens a subscription, and a loop pulls the deliveries off its stream, decodes each one, reads a field and acknowledges it; or a Repository and Routed paired into publishers. No handler, no app, no dispatch. RustStream service. The service a user writes: a #[derive(Inbox)] table, a #[subscriber] handler and RustStream::new(..).with_broker(SqlxBroker::new(pool), ..). Everything else is equal across the three: the table, the rows, the decode into the same small struct, a pool of four connections, the tokio runtime with four worker threads, and the binary. A reply scenario answers every delivery into a second table through Routed, the connected broker's default publisher. The outbox's scenarios are one app in three variants that take the three places: the app with no outbox, the same app with the outbox written by hand in raw sqlx, on the connections the crate's middleware takes, and the same app with this crate's outbox. A message published from outside a handler goes through Outbox::wrap in the last one.

A fresh table per run. Each run recreates its table and fills it, then drains it. A publish scenario writes its rows instead. The window opens at the first handled delivery and closes at the last, in all three loops, so starting the service and opening the pool stay outside it. A publish scenario's window runs from the first publish to the last. Every handled delivery counts a latch down, and the last count wakes the run, so a run knows it drained without polling the table or sleeping. The message count comes from a probe, which measures the raw loop's rate, so a measured run lasts at least five seconds on any machine. The loops are interleaved: raw, crate, service, three rounds. Each loop reports its best, median and worst round. The best is the headline, because noise only ever slows a run down. The outbox runs over Redis Pub/Sub, fed from a worker that keeps at most 1024 messages unconsumed, because Pub/Sub drops what a subscription's buffer cannot hold. A difference smaller than the spread between the rounds of either loop is indistinguishable, never a figure. A row is database-bound when round trips account for at least half of the time a message took. That is arithmetic. A probe times one statement the server answers, on one connection, before the rounds: the median of 2000 SELECT 1 round trips, published with the machine. Each scenario declares the round trips a message costs it, every statement and every connection taken from the pool, which sqlx pings before it lends one. The row is flagged when the round trip times that count reaches half the measured time per message.

Each cell drains a filled table of 20,000 rows on a pool of 16 connections, at one, four and eight workers, with single deliveries and with batches of 64. PostgreSQL and MySQL take the row lock form; SQLite, on a local file in WAL mode, takes the lease form, where a claim is one statement. The raw loop runs n tasks on one pool, each a loop that claims, reads and deletes until its claim comes back empty. The crate's loop runs n tasks on the same pool, each a broker of its own reading one subscription. The service mounts its handler with workers(n) on one subscription; one worker is the plain mount, which handles a delivery before it pulls the next. Three rounds, interleaved, and the best, median and worst of each loop.

Each scenario of the cost chart is the service a user writes, built without the testing feature, started on a single-threaded runtime against the stand's PostgreSQL, with the raw loop counted beside it. A producer on a thread and a runtime of its own fills the table between the start and the drain, so the fill is in neither count. The outbox's scenarios run over MemoryBroker, one message in flight at a time. Instructions come from callgrind and allocations from DHAT. A scenario runs over one delivery, then 1000, then 2000. The difference between the last two is the steady cost of a message, and the single delivery is the cold start. The count stops while the runtime parks waiting for the server: that work follows the server's timing, not the code. The instruction count still moves between runs, because how often a reply is still in flight when the client polls for it changes how much of sqlx's reading a message takes. Over five runs of one tree a scenario's total moved by up to about 7%, and its figure per message by up to about 15%; the scenarios that never touch the database agree to the instruction. A run against a saved baseline fails on ten percent more instructions in a scenario. Allocations do not move: each scenario declares a limit, the highest count of five full runs plus 0.1%, and every run fails above it.

just bench The recipe starts the stand from docker-compose.test.yml, PostgreSQL, MySQL and Redis in Docker on the host network, runs every scenario and the throughput grid, stops the stand and rewrites docs/benchmarks/results.json. It takes about half an hour and wants the machine to itself. RUSTSTREAM_BENCH_SECONDS sets the shortest run, RUSTSTREAM_BENCH_THROUGHPUT_ROWS the rows of a throughput cell, and RUSTSTREAM_BENCH_PAIRS the rounds. It clears RUSTFLAGS, so the binary is not tied to the CPU it was built on. Both recipes build the benchmarks the way a release is built, with fat link-time optimization across crates, so the numbers describe the code a service ships. just bench-code The code count starts the same stand and needs valgrind; it installs the benchmark runner at the release the lock file pins. just bench-code 5000 measures every scenario over five thousand deliveries instead of a thousand: a steadier figure for a longer run. just bench-code --save-baseline=main on main records a baseline, and just bench-code --baseline=main on a branch compares with it.
What the benchmark numbers of ruststream-sqlx measure, what still costs a message, and what the numbers do not allow you to conclude.

The three loops of a row are comparable with each other, because they ran in one process, interleaved, against one database. A row is not comparable with a row another broker crate publishes: a queue in a table does other work per message than a message broker, and every one of its messages is a claim, a settlement and a commit. Every number includes those round trips to the database, in all three loops. In a database-bound row they took at least half of the time a message took, so the difference between the loops is a lower bound on what the crate and the runtime do, not a measurement of it. Most inbox rows are indistinguishable: the crate's work is smaller than the spread between rounds of a loop that waits on a server. The outbox rows measure another thing: the cost of tracking. A tracked message costs an insert before its publish, and on the consumer's side a fetch and a mark, each a statement on its own connection, so the outbox against no outbox is several times slower, by design. What the crate answers for is the gap to the outbox written by hand, which runs the same statements.
documents.s: The comparison against a raw sqlx loop

documents.t: With one worker the three loops do the same work in the same order. With more, the raw loop runs n claimers, each a task that claims and deletes on its own, and the crate's loop runs n subscriptions, each on a broker of its own. A service runs one subscription for its n workers, which keeps a claim in flight for each free worker on PostgreSQL and MySQL. So the crate's column beside the raw one shows what the crate costs at the same concurrency, and the gap from the crate to the service at four and eight workers is how one subscription claims, not the dispatch. A batch takes up to its size per claim, so one claim serves that many deliveries, and the three loops stay close. On SQLite a subscription keeps one claim in flight, because SQLite takes one writer at a time, and that claim takes a row for every worker. The raw loop's n claimers on one SQLite file each claim one row at a time instead, so at four and eight workers the service claims fewer times than the raw loop for the same rows.

An instruction count holds the runtime, this crate and sqlx's driver on the service's thread: encoding each statement, the exchange with the server, decoding each row. The raw loop's count beside it is the driver's share, so the difference is the crate and the runtime. The same count costs more time where it misses the cache, so a count is not a time. Every figure is the steady state, the difference between a run of 1000 deliveries and one of 2000. Opening the pool's connections, the broker's startup checks and the first delivery are the cold start, paid once. Read an instruction figure to within a few percent, not to the digit: a service that talks to a real server moves between runs.

The crate keeps the family's rule: no allocation, dynamic call, extra atomic or copy per message on the hot path beyond sqlx's own. What remains is stated here, each where it applies: A handler that reads its delivery's transaction, Tx, pays one reference-count increment per delivery, and one that asks for the pool through Ctx<keys::Pool> pays one as well. A subscription that does not use them pays nothing. A publish through a Repository or a route reads the broker's closed flag, one atomic load, and wakes the subscriptions of its table in the process, one atomic operation each. Routed looks each message's name up, one hash lookup for an exact name, and makes one dynamic call into the row's Publish. A Repository names its table at compile time and makes neither. A by-name subscription over a row whose events are the service's own pays one boxed delivery and one boxed settlement future per message. The outbox reads a pool set after startup through a OnceLock, one atomic load per tracked message, and allocates the text of each tracked message's id header. The row lock and advisory lock forms hold one pool connection per message or batch in work: the price of a lock the database releases when its holder dies. A publish from outside a handler, through the running app's publisher, encodes each message into a buffer of its own; the raw loop keeps one buffer for every message.

The stand runs PostgreSQL and MySQL in Docker on the host network of the machine the benchmark runs on, without durability: no fsync, no flush of the log at commit. SQLite runs on a local file in WAL mode with synchronous = NORMAL. What is measured is the cost of a message, not the disk under the server. A service that keeps durability on pays for it, and pays the same in every loop. A server on another host answers a question about the network rather than about this crate. A row is one table, a small JSON body and one server on the loopback. It measures what a message costs in this crate, not what PostgreSQL, MySQL or SQLite can carry. The window closes when the last delivery is counted, before its settlement, in all three loops, so one settlement of a run sits outside the number everywhere. The numbers are a snapshot of one machine on one day, with the build recorded beside them. They are measured again by hand, on a machine given to the run alone: the differences they show are smaller than the noise of a shared one.

Where ruststream-sqlx sits: between the RustStream runtime and the service's sqlx pool, with SQL built once per subscription and the outbox beside any broker. RustStream core: Runtime: dispatch, workers, settlement, publish ruststream-sqlx: InboxSubscriber the claim loop; InboxDelivery settles its row; Repository, Routed insert rows; InboxQueue<Row> descriptor; SqlxBroker configuration; Dialect SQL per database; Outbox layers, any broker sqlx: Pool<DB> built at connect #[subscriber] handlers → Runtime: dispatch, workers, settlement, publish: mounted Runtime: dispatch, workers, settlement, publish → InboxSubscriber the claim loop: polls InboxSubscriber the claim loop → Pool<DB> built at connect Repository, Routed insert rows → Pool<DB> built at connect Pool<DB> built at connect → PostgreSQL, MySQL, MariaDB or SQLite: the driver Under the testing feature, TestApp connects in process: the same pool and database, on the test's clock The crate implements the core's broker traits over sqlx. The runtime above it is the same for every broker. Everything SQL-specific is in this crate: the InboxQueue descriptor, the claim loop, the three claim forms, what an outcome writes, and the SQL of each database. The crate subscribes, by descriptor and by name, takes batches, hands a row-mode handler the row itself, hands the partition key to keyed dispatch, publishes into tables, and describes its server in the generated document. It has no request-reply and no transactional publisher: transactional mode is a step of a subscription, where a handler writes through its delivery's transaction. The pool's settings are the service's: its size, its options and its migrations. SqlxBroker::from_url records them without I/O, so the app is built before the runtime starts; the broker builds the pool when it connects and closes it at shutdown. A service that shares one pool with code of its own builds it in its main, inside the runtime, and hands it to SqlxBroker::new, which never closes it.

A dialect builds every statement a subscription runs: PostgreSQL, MySQL and MariaDB, and SQLite are built in, an AnyPool takes the one of the database it reaches when the broker connects, and a service may bring a dialect of its own for another database. A subscription builds its statements once, when it opens, from the table's description, a const value the derive or the hand-written InboxSpec produces. So a message costs the same with the derive, the manual description or a dialect of the service's own. The startup then prepares each statement on the server, so a missing table or column stops the service before the first message.

A retry stays in its row. The descriptor declares that the database moves a delivery itself, so a retry_after is an UPDATE of the row's retry_after column, and no copy is ever published: Settlement draws it. A publish writes a row through the row type's own Publish impl. A Repository names its table at compile time. Routed, the connected broker's default publisher and so the one replies take, looks the message's name up in the routes the broker was built with. Both take the encoded bytes as a lent slice, so a reply's buffer is reused from one message to the next. What remains per message is stated by the crate and measured on Benchmarks: Routed makes one hash lookup and one dynamic call into the row's Publish. The call's future stays in a 1024-byte slot in place, and is boxed only when it is larger. A publish reads the broker's closed flag, one atomic load, and wakes the subscriptions of its table in the process, one atomic operation each. A handler that reads Tx or Ctx<keys::Pool> pays one reference-count increment per delivery. A by-name subscription over a row whose events are the service's own pays one boxed delivery and one boxed settlement future per message.

Under the testing feature, TestApp::start connects the broker in process. Nothing below the pool is replaced: the in-process broker reaches the database the test names, runs the service's SQL, its schema and its claim forms, and fails where the database fails. SQLite in memory serves a test with no server. What changes is time. The broker reads "now" from the tokio clock, anchored at the wall clock when it connected, so a test on a paused clock moves the queue's time with tb.advance(..): a retry_after row comes due when the test advances past it. Every database call runs off that clock, so a paused clock does not jump to its next timer while a reply from the database is on its way. The test clock stands in for SystemClock alone: a table on DatabaseClock reads the database's clock, and a clock of the service's own stays in force, as in production. The harness waits on the database's work through the broker's books. It counts a message when it lands in a queue a subscription of the test reads, and again when a retry returns its row, so tb.settle() returns once every row that reached a queue was delivered and settled. How the pieces start and stop is on Lifecycle, and the way of one row on Path.

One subscription keeps a claim in flight per free worker, within the pool's size less one; workers_by_key(n) keeps each partition key on one lane. a batch subscription claims a batch at a time. It counts its own deliveries in work, so the most it has seen at once tells it how many workers there are, and it keeps a claim in flight for each free one. A claim beside another starts only while the pool has a connection to spare, and the subscription never holds more than the pool's size less one: that last connection serves the handlers' own queries, their publishes and the settlements that take one. A pool short of room runs fewer deliveries at once, and subscriptions that share a pool leave each other room. After a claim that took nothing, the subscription claims one at a time until a claim takes a row again, so an empty table sees one claim per wait, not one per worker. What a delivery in work holds depends on the form. In the row lock and advisory lock forms each delivery holds a connection until it settles, so workers(n) holds up to n. In the lease form a claim and a settlement take a connection only for their statements, and the subscription takes one each half lease to extend its leases. In transactional mode every delivery holds the connection of its transaction, in every form. Size the pool for every subscription that holds connections, one more for the pool, and the connections handlers take for their own queries. Some tables keep one claim in flight at a time, where claims that run at once would cost more than they give. SQLite takes one writer at a time, so concurrent claims only collide. A FIFO table and a table with a partition_key column could see two concurrent claims finish out of claim order. On MySQL and MariaDB a lease claim stamps its rows in a transaction of several statements, which locks the rows it reads, leases in work included, until it commits. The workers still run side by side; only the claims take turns. On SQLite a lease claim takes a row for every worker the subscription has seen, in one statement. SQLite's busy handler does not queue a writer that finds the write lock taken: it sleeps a millisecond or more and tries again. A claim of one row per delivery would meet the workers' settlements at the write lock once per delivery and starve every worker while it slept. The rows past the free workers wait in the subscription for the next free worker, entered in the lease book, so their leases are extended while they wait, and a subscription that stops returns them at once. workers_by_key(n) runs n lanes, and a row goes to the lane its partition_key hashes to. The rows of one key never spread over two lanes, so they run in claim order. A FIFO group goes further: one row of a group is in work at a time, across every broker and instance that reads it, because the claim takes the group's head alone and the dialect's guard takes the group. A handler that computes runs on dedicated threads with on_threads(n). The subscription still claims on the app's runtime, and each thread queries through a small pool of its own, one connection unless set. connection_limit holds the service's pool and every thread's connections to what the database allows: a subscription that would pass it does not start. Two replicas of a service on one table share its rows without coordination: each claims on its own, and the claim form keeps a row in one place at a time.

SqlxBroker::new takes a pool the service built itself, inside the runtime, and shares with code of its own. Connect builds the pool from the recorded settings, then takes one connection of it, which checks that the database is reachable: a URL the driver cannot read fails the start with SqlxBrokerError::Url, and a database out of reach with SqlxBrokerError::Connect. On that connection the broker resolves its dialect, which matters for an AnyPool: it learns there which database it reaches. Then it gives the connection back. Under listen_notify it takes one more, which it keeps until shutdown to listen for notifications. Each subscription opens in order. Its declaration is checked first: max_attempts without dead_letter, or the other way round, and a cap on a table without an attempt column, stop it with SqlxBrokerError::Declaration. Its statements are built from the table's description, and a second subscription to the same queue on this broker is refused. Then, on one connection, the dialect reads the server's version where it has a floor, as MySQL and MariaDB do, and every statement is prepared on the server: a table or a column the database lacks stops the service at startup with SqlxBrokerError::Schema, naming the table and the statement. Last, under listen_notify, the subscription listens on its table's channel. Every error at this point is an error of startup, before a message is claimed. While the service runs, each subscription claims as Waking describes, and in the lease form a task of its own extends every lease in work each half lease. Shutdown sets the broker's closed flag, which refuses every publisher handed out before, since a pool the service shares stays open. It stops the claim loops and the lease keepers. A delivery in work in the row lock or lease form settles as before: its transaction or its lease still holds the row, and a lease is no longer extended. In the advisory lock form shutdown releases the lock of every delivery in work, and a delivery whose lock it released settles no more: its settlement fails with Closed, and its row is back in the queue. A claim the runtime cut short when it stopped a subscription may still run on the server; its connection waits for the server to end the claim's statement and roll its transaction back, and then closes. Shutdown waits for those connections and for every session still closing, closes the listening connection and the pool it built, and returns ClosedSqlxBroker, which counts the locks released with their connections back in the pool and the connections closed instead. Shutdown does not return claimed rows by itself. Each form returns them in its own way: the row lock form when its transaction rolls back or its connection closes, the lease form when a dropped delivery releases its lease or the lease runs out, the advisory lock form when its lock is released. In a service the runtime drains the handlers before it shuts the broker down, and a handler aborted at the drain timeout drops its delivery.

The outbox records each publish in a table of the service's own, on any broker, marks the record once a consumer acknowledges, and resends the rest at startup. A registry, built with outbox! or Outbox::track, names the messages it tracks and the record type each one writes. The publish layer writes a record of each tracked message through the record's own Publish impl, then sends the message with the record's id in the x-ruststream-outbox-id header. A record that fails to write fails the publish, so nothing is sent without its record. The subscription layer reads the header on the consumer's side. It fetches the record by its id, WHERE id = ? AND processed_at IS NULL where the table marks its records. A record already processed acknowledges the delivery without running the handler, which is how a copy sent twice is handled once. A fetch that fails retries the delivery without the handler. Then the handler's outcome settles the record: acknowledgement and drop mark it, with processed_at set from the database's clock or the row deleted; retry and retry_after leave it, and the record waits for the next startup. A mark that fails is logged, keeps the handler's outcome, and leaves the record for the next startup too. At startup the republish selects every unprocessed record of each name and publishes it again through the broker's publisher, with its id, once the subscriptions are open. A record the republish cannot read or send fails the startup. Two instances that start together may both send the same record, so a consumer that must not process a message twice checks that itself.

A tracked publish takes a connection of its own for the record's insert, and the record commits on it. It never joins a delivery's transaction: a record written while a transactional handler runs commits whatever the handler's outcome. The message and its record are therefore not one commit with the service's business data. What the outbox guarantees is that a publish is delivered at least once: the record is written before the send, and every send that fails or is never handled leaves a record that the next startup sends again. The usual transactional outbox, where the business row and the event row commit together and a relay polls the table, is a queue table of the inbox read by a handler that publishes on another broker.

The registry is a list in the type system, one node per registered name, so a message whose name is not registered costs one comparison of names per node and nothing else: no allocation, no database call and no dynamic call. A tracked publish takes a connection for its insert and allocates the text of the id header. A tracked delivery takes a connection for the fetch, gives it back before the handler runs, so the handler can publish tracked messages of its own, and takes one again for the mark. A pool set after the registry was built, inside #[ruststream::app], is read through a OnceLock: one atomic load per tracked message. A test build leaves the outbox off unless RUSTSTREAM_SQLX_OUTBOX=on, and a production build always tracks: the switch is compiled out of it. The pattern is the transactional outbox with the delivery side added: the consumer's mark is what ends a record, not the send.

row lock: one commit Claim: one row for each free worker → The row as the driver read it The row as the driver read it → Handler takes &Row: no codec Handler takes &Row → The outcome settles the row A claim takes rows into work by the table's claim form, and each row becomes an InboxDelivery: the row as the driver decoded it, its id, its attempt and what the form holds for it, a transaction, a lease token or a key's connection. In payload mode the codec reads the payload straight from the row's column: the bytes are lent, not copied. The headers are built on their first read, so a handler that never reads them never pays for them. A row whose payload does not decode is settled by the subscription's decode policy. In row mode the table has no payload column, and the handler takes the row itself, &Row, as the driver read it. No codec runs and nothing is copied. A batch is one claim: up to the batch size in rows, delivered together, each decoded on its own. A row that does not decode is settled by the decode policy, and the batch keeps its other rows. Each delivery of a batch settles its own row. In the row lock form the rows of a batch share the claim's transaction, so their settlements take effect together when the last one finishes, and a statement that fails rolls the whole batch back. In the lease and advisory lock forms each row settles on its own. A reply is encoded into a buffer the dispatch loop reuses, and the crate's publishers take it as a lent slice. Routed, the default reply publisher, looks the reply's name up in the broker's routes and inserts it through the row's Publish impl. Before the insert it checks that the broker is not shut down and that the table can hold every header of the message. After the insert it announces the row with pg_notify under listen_notify, and wakes the subscriptions of its table in the process. The delivery settles after the reply, as Settlement draws. Benchmarks publishes what a message costs on each of these paths, in instructions and allocations, beside a raw sqlx loop running the same statements.

A table without a group column is one queue, read by one subscription per broker The crate creates no table and runs no migration. The service writes the CREATE TABLE, and a struct describes the table to the crate: #[derive(Inbox)] reads it from attributes, and InboxTable with InboxSpec is the same description written by hand. The service's own Publish impl writes every row, so the layout of the insert stays the service's too. A row is claimable when four conditions hold, each only where the table has its column: the row is in the subscription's group, its retry_after has passed, its processed_at is empty, and no lease holds it (locked_until is empty or has passed). A claim takes claimable rows in claim order: priority first, a smaller value earlier, then retry_after, then the id. A row with a future retry_after is a scheduled job: the queue does not see it until its time comes. A subscription's name selects its queue. In a table with a group column it is the group, and every group is a queue of its own. In a table without one the name addresses the whole table. One broker opens one subscription per queue: a second subscription to the same table and group stops the service at startup with SqlxBrokerError::AlreadySubscribed. Several brokers or several instances of the service share a queue, and the claim form keeps their rows apart. What a row carries to its handler depends on two roles. With a payload column the row is in payload mode: the handler takes the payload, decoded by the codec. Without one the row is in row mode: the handler takes the row itself, as the driver read it. A headers column keeps the delivery's headers in one column, a JSON object of strings under the json feature. The headers layout reads them from columns of their own instead, each header a column. A table with neither delivers empty headers. "Now" is read when a claim selects due rows, when a retry delays a row and when an ack marks it. By default the host reads it, through SystemClock, and binds it in the column's own type. With clock = DatabaseClock the statements read the database's clock instead: Database "Now" in the statement PostgreSQL statement_timestamp() MySQL, MariaDB UTC_TIMESTAMP(6) SQLite strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%f+00:00', 'now'), text SQLite keeps times as text and compares them as text, so a table there keeps one layout of time in every row. The lease form always reads the host's clock: a lease table on DatabaseClock does not compile, for the reason Claims gives. How a claim takes a row into work is on Claims, and what each outcome writes is on Settlement.

A table with no form set takes the row lock form; a locked_until column selects the lease form; advisory_lock = ".." selects the advisory lock form. The forms differ in what holds a row while its handler runs, and so in what brings the row back when the process dies.

The claim opens a transaction and selects its rows with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. A concurrent claim skips the locked rows instead of waiting for them. The transaction stays open while the handler runs, and the settlement's statement commits it, so the row and its outcome change in one commit. When the process dies, the database rolls its transactions back and the rows are due at once. The price is one connection per delivery in work, held for the whole handler. On MySQL and MariaDB the transaction opens at READ COMMITTED unless the table names a level, so the claim locks the rows it takes and not the gaps between them.

The claim writes an expiry into locked_until, counts the attempt and commits at once, so the handler runs with no transaction open and no connection held. The subscription extends every lease in work each half lease, so a handler may run longer than its lease. The expiry is the delivery's token: a settlement names the expiry it holds, and it takes effect only while the row still holds it. A handler whose lease ran out while it ran, because its extensions failed or stopped, finds another claim's token in the row, and its settlement fails with SqlxBrokerError::LeaseLost. When the process dies, its rows return when their leases run out: thirty seconds unless set, in whole seconds. The host computes the expiry, because every settlement compares it, so a lease table reads the host's clock.

A claim selects due rows with their keys, tries each key's lock on a connection of its own without waiting, passes over a key another session holds, then takes the row while it is still claimable. Rows whose keys match go into work one at a time, so advisory_lock = "accounts-{account}" keeps each account's rows apart while other accounts run. No transaction stays open, but the connection that holds the lock stays with the delivery until it settles. When the process dies, its sessions end and the database drops their locks. A key belongs to the database, not to a table: two tables whose keys match wait for each other.

RETURNING, no order among the rows it returns Advisory lock pg_try_advisory_lock on a 64-bit hash of the key (hashtextextended, PostgreSQL 11+) GET_LOCK(name, 0) on the database's name and the key; a name past 64 characters by its SHA-256 keys kept in the process, one process per database file FIFO group guard a transaction lock on the hash of table and group a locking read of the group's unfinished rows none: one writer at a time A server older than the floor stops a subscription at startup with SqlxBrokerError::ServerTooOld: MySQL 8.0.1 and MariaDB 10.6 are the first releases that skip locked rows. A PostgreSQL advisory lock lives in the session that took it, so the form needs a direct connection or a pooler in session mode. Two processes on one SQLite file do not see each other's keys, and a row may then be delivered twice. In a FIFO table a claim takes only the head of its group, and nothing while another row of the group is in work. The guard in the table above takes the group in the claim's transaction, so subscriptions to one group on separate brokers keep its order too. The attempt is counted where the form holds the row: the row lock form counts it at settlement, in the statement that returns the row; the lease form at the claim; the advisory lock form at the take. So a crash spends an attempt in the lease and advisory lock forms, and not in the row lock form, whose rollback undoes the count with everything else. A delivery reports the attempt as it stood before its claim, so the first delivery reads 1 in every form. The databases document the primitives: PostgreSQL SELECT .. FOR UPDATE and advisory locks, MySQL locking reads and locking functions, MariaDB SKIP LOCKED.

else roll back, then settle → Unlock the key A subscription mounted with .transactional() lends its handler the delivery's transaction as Tx. Acknowledgement commits the handler's writes together with the row's settlement, so a handler's results and the end of its job are one commit. Every other outcome rolls the handler's writes back first, then settles the row as it would outside transactional mode. A row the handler inserts into a queue table through Tx commits with the acknowledgement too. A write through the pool, and a publish through the broker, commit on their own. The row lock form already holds a transaction, the claim's, so its handler writes inside it. The savepoint the subscription sets after the claim, SAVEPOINT ruststream_claim, is what lets a retry discard the handler's writes with ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT ruststream_claim and still count the attempt in the same commit. The lease and advisory lock forms commit their claims at once, so they open a transaction for the delivery after it. In the lease form the acknowledgement takes effect only while the row still holds the delivery's lease: a lost lease rolls the whole transaction back, the handler's writes with it, and the settlement fails with LeaseLost. Each delivery in transactional mode holds one connection for its transaction, in every form. A batch handler cannot be mounted with .transactional(): the step serves single deliveries.

Database Without a declaration Levels a table may declare PostgreSQL BEGIN, the server's default read_committed, repeatable_read, serializable MySQL, MariaDB READ COMMITTED all four SQLite BEGIN, deferred modes: deferred, immediate, exclusive A table declares a level with isolation = .., or a SQLite mode with mode = .., and the crate opens the row lock form's claim and every transaction of transactional mode at it. PostgreSQL runs READ UNCOMMITTED as READ COMMITTED, so its dialect does not open it, and a table that declares it does not compile against a PostgreSQL broker. SQLite runs every transaction serializable: its mode decides when a transaction takes the database's write lock, at its first write or at its start. On SQLite a delivery's transaction holds that lock until the delivery settles, and keeps every other writer out meanwhile, claims included. MySQL and MariaDB open at READ COMMITTED because their default, REPEATABLE READ, locks the gaps between the rows a locking read scans: a claim held for a handler would block every insert into the table until it ends. A row lock table on PostgreSQL at repeatable_read or serializable fails claims with serialization errors when claims and settlements of its rows run at once, so read_committed is the practical level for that form there. A lease table in transactional mode at either level stops at startup on PostgreSQL: such a transaction reads the row as its first statement found it, and would not see the lease its keeper extended since. The crate drives these transactions itself rather than through sqlx's transaction type: a transaction dropped while open closes its connection, and the server rolls it back. The levels are the databases' own: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite.

A subscription claims while its claims come back full, and otherwise waits its poll interval, which a publish of the same broker or a notification cuts short. Did the claim fill its limit? → Claim a row per free worker, or a batch: full Did the claim fill its limit? → Wait the poll interval, or less when woken: fewer rows Wait the poll interval, or less when woken → Claim a row per free worker, or a batch A publish of this broker into the table and group → Wait the poll interval, or less when woken The listening connection is back: wakes them all → Wait the poll interval, or less when woken A notification on the table's channel, on PostgreSQL → Wait the poll interval, or less when woken Another process, a trigger: pg_notify (channel, group) → A notification on the table's channel, on PostgreSQL: at commit The poll interval stays the floor under every wake-up: one second unless the broker or the subscription sets one A subscription claims when the runtime polls its stream. A claim that filled its limit is followed by the next one at once, so a backlog drains without waiting. A claim that found fewer rows than it asked for means the queue is empty for now, and the subscription waits. A claim that fails reaches the stream as an error item, and the next one waits one second, so a database out of reach cannot spin the loop. A publish through the broker wakes the subscriptions of its table on the same broker: a Repository, a route, a reply, and a message a test publishes through the harness. In a table with groups it wakes the subscriptions of its own group alone. A subscription busy with a claim keeps the wake-up for its next wait, which then returns at once. The wake-up costs a publish one atomic operation per subscription it wakes, and a subscription nothing per message. A row the service writes itself, with its own SQL or through a handler's Tx, wakes nobody: it waits for the poll interval, or for a notification.

On PostgreSQL, listen_notify makes subscriptions in other processes wake too. The broker takes one connection of the pool at connect and keeps it until shutdown, listening there. Each subscription listens on its table's channel before its first claim: the table's name, qualified with its schema where it has one, as in app.jobs. Each publish of the broker runs SELECT pg_notify(channel, group) on the connection that wrote the row, right after the write; a notification with an empty payload wakes every subscription of the table. A notification that fails is logged, and the publish still succeeds: the poll interval reaches the row. PostgreSQL delivers a notification when its transaction commits, so a woken subscription finds the row visible. A notification sent while the listening connection was lost is gone: the broker connects again and wakes every subscription once. Channel names keep 63 bytes, so a subscription to a table whose qualified name is longer stops at startup. The switch costs one connection for the broker's life and one more statement per publish. A transaction that notifies also takes a lock global to the server at commit, so notifying commits run one after another, which limits many concurrent writers. On another database listen_notify does not compile. The server documents the mechanism on NOTIFY: delivery at commit, a payload under 8000 bytes, and the 63-byte limit on identifiers. The commit lock is described by the PostgreSQL developers on the mailing list.

In the row lock form the statement runs in the claim's transaction, and its commit is the settlement: the row and its outcome change together. An event of the service's own, named with custom(..), runs its SQL in place of the dialect's statement, in the same transaction or on the same connection.

The row lock form counts it in the statement that returns the row, the lease form at the claim and the advisory lock form at the take. A handler reads the count through Ctx<keys::Attempt>, so it computes its own backoff: the crate keeps no backoff policy. The cap and its destination come together at the mount site: max_attempts(n) and dead_letter(..). A retry or a retry_after of a row whose attempt has reached the cap moves the row instead, with a warning in the log. In a table with groups the dead letter is a group, and the move is one UPDATE of the row's group. In a table without groups it is another table with the same columns: on PostgreSQL one statement, WITH moved AS (DELETE .. RETURNING ..) INSERT .. SELECT; on MySQL, MariaDB and SQLite a copy, then a delete, in one transaction. max_attempts(1) moves the row at its first failure. A delay never leaves the database. The descriptor declares that the database moves a delivery itself, so the runtime's deferred copy, which other brokers publish for a retry_after, has no use here: the row waits in the queue with its retry_after ahead, and survives a restart of the service. The outbox settles its records by the handler's outcome as well, on the consumer's side: acknowledgement and drop mark the record, a retry leaves it for the next startup, as Outbox draws.

The parts of ruststream-sqlx a service uses, one page per component: the inbox broker SqlxBroker, the queue tables it serves, the messages and headers a row hands its handler, the subscriptions and the forms they claim rows in, settlement, transactions, the context and time of a delivery, publishing and waking a subscription, the databases, the AsyncAPI document, the tests, and the transactional outbox. The crate has two halves. The inbox keeps a task queue in a table of the service's own database: a subscription claims rows, a handler's outcome settles them, and a publish writes a row through the service's own SQL. A task can then commit in the same transaction as the data it serves. The outbox is a plugin over any RustStream broker: it records what a service publishes in a table of its own until a consumer has processed it, and publishes again at startup what was not processed. The outbox needs no inbox, and a service may use both. Every feature is off by default and only adds to the crate. inbox turns the broker on and outbox the outbox. postgres, mysql (MySQL and MariaDB) and sqlite each add a built-in dialect and its sqlx driver. any serves an AnyPool, chrono or time the time columns, and json a headers column of JSON. testing adds the in-process mode a TestApp test connects, and the outbox's test switch. asyncapi adds the table a subscription reads to the generated document. any, chrono, time and asyncapi turn inbox on with them. Beside the core's required traits, the broker serves batches of rows (BatchSubscriber) and lends a handler in row mode the row itself (Carries and CarriesBatch). Its default publisher is the route table, Routed, so a reply or an Out slot without a policy of its own writes a row through a route.

With the asyncapi feature the document names the database server and, on each subscription's channel, the table it reads and its group; rows get their schema. The core builds the AsyncAPI document from the app, before anything connects. This crate adds what it knows about the parts the core describes. A server reports the database the pool reaches: its host and port and the protocol, never a credential. A channel of an InboxQueue subscription reports the table it reads under the extension x-ruststream-sqlx, with the group its name selects. Everything comes from the service's own declarations: the pool's options, the table's description and the subscription's name. A message a handler decodes is documented by its type's JsonSchema, as on every broker. A handler in row mode takes the row itself, so the row's JsonSchema documents the message: the derive names schemars through the core, #[schemars(crate = "ruststream::schemars")]. A broker made with from_url builds the document with no database in reach and no runtime.

The dependency line: ruststream-sqlx = { version = "0.7", features = ["inbox", "postgres", "asyncapi"] } The service registers its broker under the label postgres, the key of its server in the document. The tests build the document with build_spec and read it as JSON. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_asyncapi.rs fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("office", "0.1.0")).with_broker_labeled( "postgres", broker(url), |b| { b.include(send_email); b.include(render); b.include(send_mail); }, ) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { let url = env::var("DATABASE_URL").unwrap_or_else(|_| "postgres://localhost/office".to_owned()); service(&url) } examples/manual/sqlx_asyncapi.rs fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("office", "0.1.0")).with_broker_labeled( "postgres", broker(url), |b| { let email = subscriber("emails", Mailer).map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<SendEmail>::new("emails")); b.include(email.build()); let report = subscriber("reports", Renderer) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<RenderReport>::new("reports")); b.include(report.build()); let mail = subscriber("mail", Postman).map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<Mail>::new("mail")); b.include(mail.build()); }, ) } fn main() -> ExitCode { let url = env::var("DATABASE_URL").unwrap_or_else(|_| "postgres://localhost/office".to_owned()); run_main(|| service(&url)) } The mail handler takes the row of mail_jobs itself, and the message it reads is documented by the row's columns. Each InboxQueue channel carries x-ruststream-sqlx: the table it reads, qualified with its schema, and the group its name selects where the table has groups. The extension holds two fields. table is the table's name, with its schema in front where the description names one (app.email_jobs). group is the subscription's name, present only when the table has a group column: in a table without groups the name addresses the whole table. A channel the service publishes to and a subscription by name carry no extension: a name leads into a table through a route, which the channel does not describe.

The channel emails reports { "table": "app.email_jobs", "group": "emails" }, and the channel reports reports { "table": "reports" }. HandlerOutcome::ack() } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<RenderReport>::new("reports"))] async fn render(report: &Report) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(month = report.month, "rendering"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } examples/manual/sqlx_asyncapi.rs use ruststream_sqlx::dialect::Column; type Table = InboxSpec<(Payload,)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("email_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .within("app") .group(Column::new("name")) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl PayloadRow for SendEmail { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } /// One row of `reports`, a table without groups: its channel names the table alone. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct RenderReport { id: i64, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for RenderReport { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Payload,)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("reports", Column::new("id").generated()).payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl PayloadRow for RenderReport { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } struct Mailer; impl Handle<Email> for Mailer { fn handle( &self, email: &Email, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(to = %email.to, "sending"); ready(Ok(())) } } struct Renderer; impl Handle<Report> for Renderer { fn handle( &self, report: &Report, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(month = report.month, "rendering"); ready(Ok(())) } }

The server is the pool's host and port with the protocol postgres or mysql, SQLite in process with no host, an AnyPool by its scheme, never a credential. A broker registered with with_broker_labeled is a server of the document, under its label. On Postgres, MySQL and MariaDB the server is read off the URL the broker was made with, or off its pool's connect options: the host is the host and port, and the protocol is postgres or mysql. The user, the password and the database name stay out of it. SQLite runs inside the service, so its server names the protocol sqlite and no host: neither the file's path nor any other part of the URL reaches the document. An AnyPool is described by the scheme of its URL, as the broker of that database describes itself. The document is published and shared, so a password in the database's URL stays in the broker.

The broker builds its pool from the URL a deployment configures, password included; the document's server is db.internal:5432 with the protocol postgres. Macros Manual examples/sqlx_asyncapi.rs /// The broker on the database a deployment configures; it builds its pool when the service /// starts. fn broker(url: &str) -> SqlxBroker<Postgres> { SqlxBroker::from_url(url, PgPoolOptions::new().max_connections(8)) } examples/manual/sqlx_asyncapi.rs /// The broker on the database a deployment configures; it builds its pool when the service /// starts. fn broker(url: &str) -> SqlxBroker<Postgres> { SqlxBroker::from_url(url, PgPoolOptions::new().max_connections(8)) }

SqlxBroker serves the queues in the tables of the service's database through a sqlx pool; it builds the pool when it connects, or takes the service's own. SqlxBroker::from_url records the database's URL and the pool's options, and from_connect_options records the driver's connect options in place of the URL. Neither does I/O, so the service builds the broker in its #[ruststream::app] builder, before the runtime starts. connect builds the pool, and shutdown closes it. SqlxBroker::new takes a Pool<DB> the service owns and shares with the rest of its code; the broker never closes that pool. sqlx builds a pool only inside a Tokio runtime, so a service that owns its pool builds it in its own main. The database is one a built-in dialect serves: Postgres, MySQL, MariaDB or SQLite. The settings that follow the constructor are builder steps: routes that lead publishes into tables, the poll interval and the lease every subscription takes unless it names its own, and the connection limit of dedicated threads. At startup the runtime connects the broker and receives a ConnectedSqlxBroker. The connect takes one connection from the pool, so a database out of reach fails startup with SqlxBrokerError::Connect, and a URL the driver cannot read with SqlxBrokerError::Url. It also picks the dialect from that connection, which matters for an AnyPool. Every subscription then reads one queue through an InboxQueue descriptor, and the startup checks run as it opens. At shutdown the runtime turns the connected broker into a ClosedSqlxBroker. A message in work holds connections of the pool by the form its table claims rows in, and a publish takes one more; Connections shows how to size the pool.

The service serves the queue thumbnails from a SQLite file: the broker builds its pool from the file's URL, and on_startup creates the table before the subscription checks it. A test hands service a database of its own. cargo run -p ruststream-sqlx --example sqlx_broker --features inbox,sqlite,chrono,testing starts it. Each message in work holds pool connections by its form; workers(n) claims in parallel but always leaves the pool one connection for handlers. A subscription mounted with workers(n) keeps a claim in flight for each free worker. It never holds more than the pool's size less one connection, so the pool always keeps one for the handlers' own queries, their publishes and the settlements that take one. A second claim starts only while the pool has a connection to spare, so subscriptions that share a pool leave each other room, and a pool short of room runs fewer deliveries at once. A subscription keeps one claim in flight on SQLite, which takes one writer at a time, on a table whose groups keep their order, and with a partition_key column under workers_by_key(n). On SQLite that one claim takes a row for every worker in the lease form; in transactional mode each of those rows holds its transaction's connection while it waits for a worker, within the connections the subscription may hold. What a delivery holds depends on the form: Form Connections row lock one per delivery in work and one per claim in flight, for the whole handler lease one for each claim's and each settlement's statement, and one per subscription each half lease to extend the leases advisory lock one per delivery in work until it settles, in a batch too transactional mode, any form one per delivery in work, for the transaction its handler writes through A publish takes a connection of its own for its insert, and a handler that reads keys::Pool takes one for each query. So a pool is sized for every subscription: n for each workers(n), one more for the pool, and the connections the handlers take for their own work. In the lease form a pool of n + 1 lets every free worker claim at once. Under sqlx's default test_before_acquire, each acquire pings the connection first, a round trip a pool built with test_before_acquire(false) skips. Subscriptions on dedicated threads open connections of their own on top of the pool.

Four workers resize images, and each handler records its image through the pool; the pool has room for the four workers, the connection the subscription leaves free and the handlers' writes. SqlxBrokerError is the inbox's one error type: connecting, statements, the schema, declarations, leases, transactions, publishes, and a closed broker. Every variant about a subscription names the subscription, the table and the row type, so one line of a log says where to look. The database's own error is its source. Variant When Connect the connect could not take a connection from the pool Url the connect could not read the URL of a broker made with from_url Backend an AnyPool reached a database whose dialect's feature is off Schema a statement failed to prepare at startup: the table lacks a table or a column the description names Dialect the dialect could not build a statement for the table ServerTooOld the server is older than the statements of the table's form need Declaration the mount declared what the table cannot carry ConnectionLimit a subscription on dedicated threads would pass the broker's connection limit AlreadySubscribed a second subscription to one queue on the same broker Sqlx a statement failed while the subscription ran BatchRolledBack an earlier settlement of a batch failed, so the batch rolls back LeaseLost in the lease form, the lease ran out and another claim took the row, so the settlement took no effect TransactionHeld in transactional mode, the handler kept its transaction past its return Listen listen_notify could not listen on the table's channel Publish the service's Publish failed Header the publish carries a header the table cannot hold byte for byte NoRoute no route leads the name to a table Closed the broker was shut down, and a handle outlived it A service meets the error in three places. A failed startup carries it as the source of the runtime's error, and the service exits before it reads a row. A publish from a handler returns it inside the core's PublishError, and the handler decides how its delivery settles. A settlement that fails, such as LeaseLost, goes to the log with the row's id. The enum is #[non_exhaustive], so a match on it ends with a wildcard arm.

An invoice the database refuses to write is logged with its cause, and the payment waits a minute before it is billed again. One glob, ruststream_sqlx::prelude, brings the core prelude, the derives, the broker, InboxQueue, its steps, the publish policies and the keys. use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; is the one import a service on the inbox writes. It carries the core's own prelude, so #[subscriber], RustStream, HandlerOutcome and Out come with it. It adds the derives Inbox and InboxHeaders, the broker SqlxBroker, the descriptor InboxQueue, the mount steps of InboxSettings and InboxThreads, the traits Insert and Publish, the publish policies Repository and Routed, and the keys a handler reads. Publish here is the trait a table implements to receive a publish, not a policy. Another broker's prelude may name its publish policy Publish, so a file that imports both globs names one of them by its path. The rest is imported by path: the event traits such as Ack and Fetch, DatabaseClock, HeaderColumn, the dialect and spec modules a table described by hand uses, and everything of the outbox.

The descriptor with its poll interval, the attempt key, the derive, the routes and the Routed policy of an Out slot all come from the one glob. Shutdown returns ClosedSqlxBroker, releases every advisory lock in work, and a publisher kept past it reports SqlxBrokerError::Closed. At shutdown the runtime first stops the subscriptions and lets the handlers in work finish, up to its shutdown timeout. Then it shuts the broker down: the claim loops stop, and so does the extension of the leases. A claim the runtime cut short as it stopped a subscription may still run on the server; shutdown waits until the server has ended it and rolled its transaction back, so the stopped service holds no lock on the table. A delivery in work in the lease form keeps its lease, which runs out unless the delivery settles first; its row then returns to the queue. In the advisory lock form the broker releases the lock of every delivery in work and waits for the settlements in flight, so no lock of the broker is left. A pool the broker built (from_url) closes last: it lends no new connection, and a connection a delivery in work still holds closes when it comes back. A settlement after the shutdown that needs a new connection, as in the lease form, then fails, and its row returns when its lease runs out. The service's own pool (new) stays open, and the service closes it after run returns. A handle taken before shutdown, such as a repository publisher, refuses every publish afterwards with SqlxBrokerError::Closed, and never writes a row past the shutdown. A tool that drives the broker by hand receives the ClosedSqlxBroker, whose locks_released and connections_closed count what the shutdown did to the advisory locks.

run returns once the handlers have drained and the broker has shut down and closed the pool it built. A subscription builds and prepares its statements when it opens, so a missing table or column, a retry the table cannot carry or a second reader stops startup. A struct that cannot drive a queue does not compile at all; the derive lists those errors. What only the database can tell is checked at startup. Each subscription builds its statements with the broker's dialect and prepares each one on the server. A table or a column the description names and the database lacks fails startup with SqlxBrokerError::Schema, which names the subscription, the table and the statement. Preparing checks names, not column types: a row whose columns do not decode reaches the decode policy instead. The other refusals at startup: Error When Declaration the mount declares what the table cannot carry: max_attempts(n) without dead_letter(..) or the reverse, a cap on a table without an attempt column, or transactional mode in the lease form at a strict isolation level on Postgres Dialect the dialect cannot build a statement the table needs ServerTooOld a MySQL older than 8.0.1 or a MariaDB older than 10.6, which lack SKIP LOCKED AlreadySubscribed a second subscription to one queue on the same broker; a table without a group column is one queue Connect, Backend the broker could not take a connection, or an AnyPool reached a database whose dialect feature is off The service runs its migrations before the app starts, and the checks then see the schema the release reads.

A release adds an attempt column to the queue; on_startup applies the schema before the subscriptions open, and a table without the column stops startup with SqlxBrokerError::Schema.
