In the manual form, InboxSpec says the same. InboxQueue::<MakeThumbnail>::new("thumbnails") is the subscription: it claims rows of thumbnail_jobs and hands each payload to the codec. What the handler returns settles the row: ack() deletes it, and drop() finishes it the same way without a thumbnail. Ctx<keys::Attempt> reads which delivery of the row this is. service takes the database's URL. SqlxBroker::from_url records it with the pool's options and connects nothing, so the app is built before the runtime starts. on_startup creates the table before the subscription checks it. A publish to thumbnails writes a row. route leads the name to MakeThumbnail, and the service's own Publish statement inserts it. A handler's reply or a test publishes the same way. Code outside a handler, such as an HTTP endpoint, writes the row with the derive's insert, inside its own transaction: Enqueueing jobs shows it.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service("sqlite:thumbnails.db?mode=rwc") } src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service("sqlite:thumbnails.db?mode=rwc") } #[ruststream::app] generates main, which builds the app and runs it. The broker builds its pool when the service starts, and closes it when the service stops. cargo run The service claims rows as they appear in thumbnails.db. A row another program inserts is seen within the poll interval, one second unless set. Ctrl+C stops it.

The example file also holds two tests. Each opens a SQLite database in memory and starts the same service on it with TestApp::start. A test publishes an image through the route, as production does, and checks how thumbnail settled it and what is left in the table: cargo test Testing a service on SQL walks through these tests.

The same struct serves a PgPool or a MySqlPool: the broker takes the dialect of its pool. Turn on postgres or mysql in both crates, build that pool, and write Publish<Postgres> or Publish<MySql> with the database's placeholders. On a server, a table without locked_until claims its rows under a row lock, held while the handler runs. Index the claim order, (group, priority, retry_after, id) for the columns the table has; Running in production explains why.

A queue on sqlx usually is a loop of SELECT .. FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED and a few columns of bookkeeping. Here is where each part goes: Hand-written ruststream-sqlx the claim loop and its statement an InboxQueue subscription; the dialect builds the statement DELETE or UPDATE .. SET done after the work the handler's outcome an attempts column raised by hand #[field(attempt)] and Ctx<keys::Attempt> a run_at column for later #[field(retry_after)] and retry_after(d) (Retries) a locked_until column and a reaper the lease form (Long jobs) a dead-letter table and its move max_attempts(n) and dead_letter a job inserted with the data it serves insert in the same transaction (Enqueueing jobs)

This guide keeps jobs in order: all the jobs of a group, or the jobs of each key while other keys run in parallel. SKIP LOCKED makes claims fast because they pass over rows in work. It also lets the next row go out while an earlier one is still in work or waiting for its retry. A queue whose jobs must apply in order says so in its table. The example is an accounts service. It sends contact changes to a CRM, which must receive them in the order they happened, and applies ledger postings, which must keep their order within an account.
documents.s: Ordering: FIFO groups and partition keys

documents.t: src/main.rs const SCHEMA: &str = " CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS crm_jobs ( id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, target TEXT NOT NULL, attempt INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1, locked_until TEXT, payload BLOB NOT NULL ); CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS crm_jobs_claim ON crm_jobs (target, id); CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS ledger_jobs ( id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, account TEXT NOT NULL, locked_until TEXT, payload BLOB NOT NULL ); "; The index on crm_jobs follows the claim order, the group first. A claim of a FIFO group reads the group's unfinished rows, and the index keeps that read to them (Running in production).

Macros Manual src/main.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::Connection; use sqlx::Sqlite; use sqlx::sqlite::SqlitePoolOptions; /// One row of `crm_jobs`; each group holds the changes bound for one system, in order. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "crm_jobs")] struct CrmChange { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(group, fifo = true)] target: String, #[field(attempt, generated)] attempt: i16, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } /// The CRM receives its changes one at a time, in the order they were queued. #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<CrmChange>::new("crm"))] async fn sync(change: &Contact) -> HandlerOutcome { if push(change).await { return HandlerOutcome::ack(); } // At once: the change keeps its place at the head of the group. HandlerOutcome::retry() } src/main.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::Connection; use sqlx::Sqlite; use sqlx::sqlite::SqlitePoolOptions; /// One row of `crm_jobs`; each group holds the changes bound for one system, in order. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct CrmChange { id: i64, attempt: i16, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for CrmChange { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Fifo, Attempt, Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("crm_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .fifo_group(Column::new("target")) .attempt(Column::new("attempt").generated()) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl AttemptRow for CrmChange { type Attempt = i16; fn attempt(&self) -> &i16 { &self.attempt } } impl PayloadRow for CrmChange { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } /// The CRM receives its changes one at a time, in the order they were queued. struct PushToCrm; impl Handle<Contact> for PushToCrm { async fn handle( &self, change: &Contact, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { if push(change).await { return Ok(()); } // At once: the change keeps its place at the head of the group. Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()) } } #[field(group, fifo = true)] makes each group of target a FIFO group. A FIFO group has at most one row in work, however many workers, subscriptions and processes read it. Its first unfinished row in claim order is its head, and a claim takes the head alone. The rows behind it wait while the head is in work, under a lease of another instance included. retry() keeps the change at the head, so it goes again before the ones behind it. retry_after(d) would move it behind the rows due before it. A head that keeps failing holds its whole group. The mount caps it: Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The service on the database `url` names. fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); // Nothing connects here: the broker builds its pool when the service starts. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, SqlitePoolOptions::new()); let broker = broker .route::<CrmChange>("crm") .route::<LedgerPosting>("postings"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("accounts", "0.1.0")) // The table, created before the subscription checks it. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = SqliteConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // A change the CRM refuses three times moves out of the group, which then moves on. b.include(sync) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("crm.parked"); // Four workers, and the postings of one account on one of them, one after another. b.include(post.workers_by_key(nonzero!(4))); }) } src/main.rs /// The service on the database `url` names. fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); // Nothing connects here: the broker builds its pool when the service starts. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, SqlitePoolOptions::new()); let broker = broker .route::<CrmChange>("crm") .route::<LedgerPosting>("postings"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("accounts", "0.1.0")) // The table, created before the subscription checks it. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = SqliteConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // A change the CRM refuses three times moves out of the group, which then moves on. let sync = subscriber("crm", PushToCrm).map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<CrmChange>::new("crm")); b.include(sync.build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(3u32)) .dead_letter("crm.parked"); // Four workers, and the postings of one account on one of them, one after another. let post = subscriber("postings", Post) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<LedgerPosting>::new("postings")) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(4)); b.include(post.build()); }) } After three refusals the change moves into the crm.parked group, and the next change of crm becomes the head. A parked change waits there for a person; the changes behind it have gone out without it, and that is the price of freeing the group. Groups run side by side, each through a subscription of its own, so a group suits a few streams known in advance: one per downstream system, one per tenant. workers(n) gives a FIFO subscription no parallelism, and one worker serves it.

A ledger has many accounts, too many for a subscription each. The order that matters is within one account, and accounts may run in parallel. Macros Manual src/main.rs /// One row of `ledger_jobs`: the postings of one account apply in the order they were written. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "ledger_jobs")] struct LedgerPosting { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(partition_key)] account: String, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<LedgerPosting>::new("postings"))] async fn post(posting: &Posting) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(account = %posting.account, posting.n, "posting"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs /// One row of `ledger_jobs`: the postings of one account apply in the order they were written. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct LedgerPosting { id: i64, account: String, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for LedgerPosting { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Key, Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("ledger_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .partition_key(Column::new("account")) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl KeyRow for LedgerPosting { type Key = String; fn partition_key(&self) -> &String { &self.account } } impl PayloadRow for LedgerPosting { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } struct Post; impl Handle<Posting> for Post { fn handle( &self, posting: &Posting, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(account = %posting.account, posting.n, "posting"); ready(Ok(())) } } #[field(partition_key)] gives each row the account as its key. The app mounts post with workers_by_key(4): four workers, and the postings of one account on one of them, in the order they were claimed. The subscription keeps one claim in flight on such a table, so the claims do not overtake each other. That order holds inside one subscription. Postings of one account that must stay in order across several instances go into a FIFO group, or into the advisory lock form with a key on the account, which keeps the rows of one key in work one at a time across every process on a server.

The tests in the example file run the service on SQLite in memory. The first publishes a change the CRM refuses and one it takes: the first goes three times and is parked, then the second goes out. The second writes the head of crm as leased by another instance and finds that the change behind it waits. The third writes postings of two accounts, interleaved, and finds each account's postings applied in order. The rows of the last two tests wake no subscription, so they run on the real clock with TestApp::start_live past the poll interval.

This guide makes every message a service publishes reach a handler that processes it, on a broker that keeps nothing. Some brokers deliver a message only to whoever listens at that moment, Redis Pub/Sub and NATS core among them, and a consumer may stop halfway through any message. The outbox records each message the service publishes under a registered name, marks the record once a consumer processed the message, and publishes the unprocessed records again at startup. It is a plugin over any RustStream broker and needs no relay process. Its outbox feature is independent of the inbox. The example takes payments at checkout and ships the paid orders, over the in-memory broker.
documents.s: Tracking what you publish: the outbox plugin

documents.t: src/main.rs const SCHEMA: &str = "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS outbox ( id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, payload BLOB NOT NULL, processed_at TEXT )"; The table is the service's: it creates it, with its own migrations in production. processed_at stays empty until a consumer processed the message.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use ruststream_sqlx::{Outbox, outbox}; /// One record of the `outbox` table. #[derive(Outbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[outbox(table = "outbox")] struct PaymentOutbox { #[field(id)] id: i64, #[field(name)] name: String, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, #[field(processed_at)] processed_at: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, } /// The service writes the record and returns its id; the outbox sends the id with the message. impl outbox::Publish<Sqlite> for PaymentOutbox { async fn publish(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, msg: &OutgoingMessage<'_>) -> sqlx::Result<i64> { sqlx::query_scalar("INSERT INTO outbox (name, payload) VALUES (?, ?) RETURNING id") .bind(msg.name()) .bind(msg.payload()) .fetch_one(conn) .await } } src/main.rs use ruststream_sqlx::outbox::{self, Outbox}; /// One record of the `outbox` table. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct PaymentOutbox { id: i64, name: String, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl OutboxTable for PaymentOutbox { type Id = i64; type Table = OutboxSpec<(ProcessedAt,)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = OutboxSpec::new( "outbox", Column::new("id"), Column::new("name"), Column::new("payload"), ) .processed_at(Column::new("processed_at")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } fn name(&self) -> &str { &self.name } fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } /// The name `PaymentTaken` is published under. struct Payments; impl TrackedName for Payments { const NAME: &'static str = "payments"; } /// The service writes the record and returns its id; the outbox sends the id with the message. impl outbox::Publish<Sqlite> for PaymentOutbox { async fn publish(conn: &mut SqliteConnection, msg: &OutgoingMessage<'_>) -> sqlx::Result<i64> { sqlx::query_scalar("INSERT INTO outbox (name, payload) VALUES (?, ?) RETURNING id") .bind(msg.name()) .bind(msg.payload()) .fetch_one(conn) .await } } #[derive(Outbox)] describes the record: id, name and payload are required, headers and processed_at optional. The service writes the record with its own outbox::Publish and returns its id; the crate builds the other statements. In the manual form, OutboxSpec says the same, and a TrackedName type names what is tracked.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; /// The reply to `payments` is recorded before it is sent. #[subscriber("checkout", reply)] async fn take_payment(checkout: &Checkout) -> PaymentTaken { tracing::info!(order = checkout.order, "payment taken"); PaymentTaken { order: checkout.order, } } /// The acknowledgement marks the payment's record processed. #[subscriber("payments")] async fn ship(payment: &PaymentTaken) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(order = payment.order, "shipping"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs use ruststream::memory::prelude::*; use sqlx::SqlitePool; /// The reply to `payments` is recorded before it is sent. struct TakePayment; // The app's state is the pool `on_startup` returns. impl Handle<Checkout, PaymentTaken, (), (), SqlitePool> for TakePayment { fn handle( &self, checkout: &Checkout, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), SqlitePool>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<PaymentTaken, HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order = checkout.order, "payment taken"); ready(Ok(PaymentTaken { order: checkout.order, })) } } /// The acknowledgement marks the payment's record processed. struct Ship; impl Handle<PaymentTaken, (), (), (), SqlitePool> for Ship { fn handle( &self, payment: &PaymentTaken, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_, (), SqlitePool>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(order = payment.order, "shipping"); ready(Ok(())) } } The handlers know nothing of the outbox: the middlewares of the app do the tracking.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use std::convert::Infallible; use std::io; use sqlx::SqlitePool; fn service(url: String) -> impl App { // The registry starts without a pool: sqlx builds one only inside the Tokio runtime. let tracking = outbox! { "payments" => PaymentOutbox }; let registry = tracking.clone(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| { let pool = SqlitePool::connect(&url).await.map_err(io::Error::other)?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA) .execute(&pool) .await .map_err(io::Error::other)?; registry.set_pool(pool.clone()).map_err(io::Error::other)?; Ok::<_, io::Error>(pool) }) .layer(tracking.layer()) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .after_shutdown(async move |pool| { pool.close().await; Ok::<_, Infallible>(()) }) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(take_payment).out_reply(Publish); b.include(ship); // Once the subscriptions are open, the unprocessed records are sent again. b.after_startup(Publish, tracking.republish()); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service("sqlite:payments.db?mode=rwc".to_owned()) } src/main.rs use std::convert::Infallible; use std::io; fn service(url: String) -> impl App { // The registry starts without a pool: sqlx builds one only inside the Tokio runtime. let tracking = Outbox::deferred().track::<PaymentOutbox, Payments>(); let registry = tracking.clone(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("payments", "0.1.0")) .on_startup(async move |()| { let pool = SqlitePool::connect(&url).await.map_err(io::Error::other)?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA) .execute(&pool) .await .map_err(io::Error::other)?; registry.set_pool(pool.clone()).map_err(io::Error::other)?; Ok::<_, io::Error>(pool) }) .layer(tracking.layer()) .publish_layer(tracking.publish_layer()) .after_shutdown(async move |pool| { pool.close().await; Ok::<_, Infallible>(()) }) .with_broker(MemoryBroker::new(), |b| { b.include(subscriber("checkout", TakePayment).reply().build()) .out_reply(Publish); b.include(subscriber("payments", Ship).build()); // Once the subscriptions are open, the unprocessed records are sent again. b.after_startup(Publish, tracking.republish()); }) } #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { service("sqlite:payments.db?mode=rwc".to_owned()) } outbox! registers payments with its record; a name registered twice does not compile. #[ruststream::app] builds the app before the Tokio runtime exists, and sqlx builds a pool only inside one. So the registry starts without a pool, and on_startup builds the pool and hands it over with set_pool; after_shutdown closes it. A tracked message goes through four steps: The publish layer writes the record, then sends the message with the record's id in the x-ruststream-outbox-id header. A record that cannot be written fails the publish. The subscription layer takes a delivery that carries an id into work by that id and runs the handler; a copy whose record is processed already is acknowledged without the handler. The handler's acknowledgement or drop marks the record processed; a retry leaves it as it was. At startup, republish sends every unprocessed record again, once the subscriptions are open. The consumer marks the record in the producer's table, so producer and consumer share the registry and the database, as both handlers in one app do here.

A message is delivered at least once. The record is written before the message is sent, so a failed send, a consumer that stops mid-handler, or a handler that asks for the message again leaves the record for the next startup. Two instances that start together may both send the same record again, so a consumer that must not process a message twice checks that itself. The record is written on a connection of its own and commits at once. It does not join a transaction of the service: a transactional inbox handler that is retried discards its own writes and keeps the record of what it published. On SQLite such a handler publishes before its first write through its transaction, because the record's insert needs that transaction's write lock; a publish after that write fails with OutboxError::WriteLockHeld (Interplay). An event that must commit with the business rows is a row of the business transaction, relayed afterwards: Relaying events to another broker. A publish outside a handler, an HTTP endpoint for one, takes the running app's publisher and wraps it in the registry, so it is tracked the same way. The tracking costs a connection for each tracked publish, and two for each tracked delivery: one for the fetch, one for the settlement. A message under a name the registry does not hold costs a comparison of names. The repository's examples/outbox runs the same flow over Redis Pub/Sub, with migrations and a fetch of its own.

A test build leaves the outbox off unless RUSTSTREAM_SQLX_OUTBOX=on turns it on (Switch), so a service's own tests run its handlers untracked. The tests in the example file that check the tracking skip without the switch; one more test checks that the service runs untracked with it off: cargo test RUSTSTREAM_SQLX_OUTBOX=on cargo test With the switch on, one test checks that a payment is recorded, sent with its record's id, and marked once shipped. Another writes a record an earlier instance left unprocessed and finds it shipped after the startup. Both run with TestApp::start on a SQLite database in memory, which the service's own pool opens by its URL.

This guide takes a queue to production on Postgres: the schema and its index, the checks that catch a wrong schema, the pool, the database versions and poolers, and shutdown. The service is a mailer with eight workers, a cap of five attempts and a dead-letter group.

src/main.rs /// The service's first migration; in a service crate, `migrations/0001_email_jobs.sql`, run by /// `sqlx::migrate!`. const MIGRATION: &str = " CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS email_jobs ( job_id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, attempt SMALLINT NOT NULL DEFAULT 1, payload BYTEA NOT NULL ); CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS email_jobs_claim ON email_jobs (name, job_id); "; The crate creates no table: the schema is the service's, and its migrations create it, as sqlx::migrate! runs them in examples/outbox. The index follows the claim order, (group, priority, retry_after, id) for the columns the table has, (name, job_id) here. A claim locks every row of its group it reads before it sorts them, so without that index a claim held for a handler keeps the rest of its group from other claims. In a table with FIFO groups the same index keeps the claim's read of the group to the group's own rows.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::Postgres; /// One row of `email_jobs`: every statement it determines goes through sqlx's compile-time check. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "email_jobs", checked, db = postgres)] struct SendEmail { #[field(id, generated)] job_id: i64, #[field(group)] name: String, #[field(attempt, generated)] attempt: i16, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } src/main.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::Postgres; /// One row of `email_jobs`, claimed by row lock: the description names no other form. Each /// subscription prepares its statements at startup; the compile-time check is the derive's. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct SendEmail { job_id: i64, attempt: i16, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for SendEmail { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Attempt, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("email_jobs", Column::new("job_id").generated()) .group(Column::new("name")) .attempt(Column::new("attempt").generated()) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.job_id } } impl AttemptRow for SendEmail { type Attempt = i16; fn attempt(&self) -> &i16 { &self.attempt } } impl PayloadRow for SendEmail { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } checked, db = postgres hands every statement the struct determines to sqlx's compile-time check: the claim, the settlements, the dead letter of a group and the insert. A column the struct names and the table lacks fails the build. The build checks against DATABASE_URL, or against the .sqlx data that cargo sqlx prepare writes, committed beside the crate; cargo sqlx prepare --check in CI fails a build whose data is stale. The subscription runs the same statements it runs without checked, so a message costs the same. The check is the derive's: a table described by hand keeps the startup check alone. Every subscription also prepares its statements at startup. A table or column the database lacks stops the service with SqlxBrokerError::Schema, which names the subscription, the table and the statement. A mount that declares a cap without its dead letter, or the reverse, stops it too. So on_startup runs the migrations before the subscriptions open, and the checks see the schema the release reads.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use std::num::NonZeroUsize; use std::time::Duration; use sqlx::Connection; use sqlx::postgres::{PgConnectOptions, PgPoolOptions}; /// The emails in work at once; each holds its row's lock and a connection until it settles. const WORKERS: NonZeroUsize = nonzero!(8); /// A connection for each worker, and one the subscription leaves to settlements and publishes. fn pool() -> PgPoolOptions { let size = u32::try_from(WORKERS.get() + 1).unwrap_or(u32::MAX); PgPoolOptions::new() .max_connections(size) .acquire_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5)) } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<SendEmail>::new("emails"))] async fn send(email: &Email, Ctx(attempt): Ctx<keys::Attempt>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(to = %email.to, ?attempt, "sending"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } /// The service on the database `options` reach. fn service(options: PgConnectOptions) -> RustStream { let migrate = options.clone(); // Nothing connects here: the broker builds its pool when the service starts. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_connect_options(options, pool()).route::<SendEmail>("emails"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("mailer", "0.1.0")) // The schema the release reads exists before any subscription prepares its statements. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = PgConnection::connect_with(&migrate).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(MIGRATION).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) // The label names the server in the generated AsyncAPI document. .with_broker_labeled("postgres", broker, |b| { b.include(send.workers(WORKERS)) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("emails.dead"); }) } src/main.rs use std::num::NonZeroUsize; use std::time::Duration; use sqlx::Connection; use sqlx::postgres::{PgConnectOptions, PgPoolOptions}; /// The emails in work at once; each holds its row's lock and a connection until it settles. const WORKERS: NonZeroUsize = nonzero!(8); /// A connection for each worker, and one the subscription leaves to settlements and publishes. fn pool() -> PgPoolOptions { let size = u32::try_from(WORKERS.get() + 1).unwrap_or(u32::MAX); PgPoolOptions::new() .max_connections(size) .acquire_timeout(Duration::from_secs(5)) } struct Mailer; impl Handle<Email, (), (), InboxContext> for Mailer { async fn handle( &self, email: &Email, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, InboxContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Ctx(attempt) = Ctx::<keys::Attempt>::from_context(ctx).await?; tracing::info!(to = %email.to, ?attempt, "sending"); Ok(()) } } /// The service on the database `options` reach. fn service(options: PgConnectOptions) -> RustStream { let migrate = options.clone(); // Nothing connects here: the broker builds its pool when the service starts. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_connect_options(options, pool()).route::<SendEmail>("emails"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("mailer", "0.1.0")) // The schema the release reads exists before any subscription prepares its statements. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = PgConnection::connect_with(&migrate).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(MIGRATION).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) // The label names the server in the generated AsyncAPI document. .with_broker_labeled("postgres", broker, |b| { let send = subscriber("emails", Mailer) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<SendEmail>::new("emails")) .workers(WORKERS); b.include(send.build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("emails.dead"); }) } The table names no form, so it claims by row lock: each email in work holds its row's lock and a connection until it settles. A subscription never holds more than the pool's size less one, and leaves that one to the handlers' own queries, their publishes and the settlements. So the pool is sized for every subscription of the service: n for each workers(n), one more, and the connections the handlers take for their own work (Connections). A lease table holds a connection only for each statement, and suits a pool that cannot spare one per job. On Postgres, notifications keep one more connection for the broker's life. pool returns the pool's options, and the broker builds the pool from them when the service starts. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[ruststream::app] fn app() -> impl App { // The connection's settings come from the `PG*` environment variables. service(PgConnectOptions::new()) } src/main.rs fn main() -> ExitCode { // The connection's settings come from the `PG*` environment variables. run_main(|| service(PgConnectOptions::new())) }

Database Needs Postgres 9.5 for SKIP LOCKED; 11 for the advisory lock form and FIFO groups, which lock 64-bit hashes MySQL, MariaDB MySQL 8.0.1 or MariaDB 10.6, read at startup; an older server stops it with ServerTooOld SQLite the lease or the advisory lock form; one process per database file in the advisory form On MySQL and MariaDB a claim runs at READ COMMITTED unless a row lock table declares another level. A server that logs statements, binlog_format = STATEMENT, refuses writes at that level; the row and mixed formats accept them. On Postgres read_committed is the practical isolation level of a row lock table: a stricter level fails claims with serialization errors when claims and settlements run at once. The advisory lock form keeps its lock in the database session, so it needs a direct connection or PgBouncer in session pooling; transaction pooling hands the session to another client between statements. A broker with listen_notify listens on a session too.

At shutdown the runtime stops the subscriptions, lets the handlers in work finish within its shutdown timeout, then shuts the broker down. A row lock delivery holds its transaction until it settles; one still unsettled when the process exits rolls back with its connection, and its row returns. A lease delivery keeps its lease and settles if it can, or its row returns when the lease runs out. The broker releases the advisory locks of the deliveries in work. The broker closes the pool it built last; a connection a delivery in work still holds closes when it comes back.

With the asyncapi feature, the generated AsyncAPI document describes the server and each subscription's table and group. The label of with_broker_labeled names the server, and the server entry holds the database's host and port, never its user or password: the document is published and shared.

One test in the example file builds the document of the service on a URL with a password, with no I/O, and finds the host and port in it and the password nowhere. Two more run against a Postgres database of their own: a table of an older release, without a column the struct names, stops the startup with an error that names it, and the checked statements serve the queue. They read the server's address from POSTGRES_TEST_URL and skip without it (Testing a service on SQL).

This guide writes an event in the same transaction as the data it describes, then publishes it to another broker. A service that saves an order and then publishes "order placed" to Kafka has two writes that can part. The order can commit while the publish fails, or the publish can go out for an order that rolled back. The transactional outbox joins them: the event is a row written in the order's transaction, and a relay publishes the rows that committed. With this crate the event table is a queue table, and the relay is an ordinary subscription. The example is a shop. A checkout places the order and writes its event; the relay publishes each event to a bus, the in-memory broker here.

src/main.rs const SCHEMA: &str = " CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS orders (id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, total_cents INTEGER NOT NULL); CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS checkout_jobs ( id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, locked_until TEXT, payload BLOB NOT NULL ); CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS order_events ( id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, aggregate TEXT NOT NULL, locked_until TEXT, payload BLOB NOT NULL ); "; Macros Manual src/main.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::Connection; use sqlx::sqlite::SqlitePoolOptions; use sqlx::{Sqlite, SqliteConnection}; /// One row of `order_events`: an event waiting for the relay, keyed by its order. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "order_events")] struct OrderEvent { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(partition_key)] aggregate: String, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } /// The order and its event, in the checkout's transaction: both commit, or neither does. async fn place( conn: &mut SqliteConnection, order: &Order, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { sqlx::query("INSERT INTO orders (id, total_cents) VALUES (?, ?)") .bind(order.id) .bind(order.total_cents) .execute(&mut *conn) .await?; let placed = OrderPlaced { order: order.id, total_cents: order.total_cents, }; let event = OrderEvent { id: 0, aggregate: order.id.to_string(), locked_until: None, payload: serde_json::to_vec(&placed)?, }; event.insert(conn).await?; Ok(()) } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<Checkout>::new("checkouts"))] async fn checkout(order: &Order, Ctx(mut tx): Ctx<keys::Tx<Sqlite>>) -> HandlerOutcome { match place(&mut tx, order).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), Err(error) => { tracing::warn!(subscription = "checkouts", order.id, %error, "order not placed"); HandlerOutcome::drop() } } } src/main.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::Connection; use sqlx::sqlite::SqlitePoolOptions; use sqlx::{Sqlite, SqliteConnection}; /// One row of `order_events`: an event waiting for the relay, keyed by its order. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct OrderEvent { id: i64, aggregate: String, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for OrderEvent { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Key, Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("order_events", Column::new("id").generated()) .partition_key(Column::new("aggregate")) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl KeyRow for OrderEvent { type Key = String; fn partition_key(&self) -> &String { &self.aggregate } } impl PayloadRow for OrderEvent { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } // INSERT INTO `order_events` (`aggregate`, `locked_until`, `payload`) VALUES (?, ?, ?) const INSERT: Sql<160> = insert::sqlite(&OrderEvent::TABLE.spec()); impl Insert<SqliteConnection> for OrderEvent { async fn insert(&self, conn: &mut SqliteConnection) -> Result<(), sqlx::Error> { sqlx::query(INSERT.as_str()) .bind(&self.aggregate) .bind(None::<DateTime<Utc>>) .bind(&self.payload) .execute(conn) .await?; Ok(()) } } /// The order and its event, in the checkout's transaction: both commit, or neither does. async fn place( conn: &mut SqliteConnection, order: &Order, ) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error + Send + Sync>> { sqlx::query("INSERT INTO orders (id, total_cents) VALUES (?, ?)") .bind(order.id) .bind(order.total_cents) .execute(&mut *conn) .await?; let placed = OrderPlaced { order: order.id, total_cents: order.total_cents, }; let event = OrderEvent { id: 0, aggregate: order.id.to_string(), payload: serde_json::to_vec(&placed)?, }; event.insert(conn).await?; Ok(()) } struct PlaceOrder; impl Handle<Order, (), (), TxContext<Sqlite>> for PlaceOrder { async fn handle( &self, order: &Order, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, TxContext<Sqlite>>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Ctx(mut tx) = Ctx::<keys::Tx<Sqlite>>::from_context(ctx).await?; place(&mut tx, order).await.map_err(|error| { tracing::warn!(subscription = "checkouts", order.id, %error, "order not placed"); HandlerOutcome::drop() }) } } checkout runs in transactional mode: it writes the order and the event through its delivery's transaction. Its acknowledgement commits both with the checkout's settlement. An order whose insert fails rolls its event back, and nothing is published for it. Code outside a handler, an HTTP endpoint for one, writes the same two rows in a sqlx transaction of its own, as Enqueueing jobs does. The event row wakes no subscription in that case either: the relay finds it within its poll interval.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use ruststream::memory::{MemoryBroker, MemoryPublish}; /// Each event goes out on the bus as it was written; the acknowledgement deletes its row. #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<OrderEvent>::new("order-events"), reply)] async fn relay(event: &OrderPlaced) -> OrderPlaced { event.clone() } /// The service on the database `url` names. fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); // Nothing connects here: the broker builds its pool when the service starts. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, SqlitePoolOptions::new()); // The target broker is wrapped first, so its publish token exists before the scopes. let bus = MemoryBroker::new().bindable(); let to_bus = bus.bind(MemoryPublish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")) // The table, created before the subscription checks it. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = SqliteConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker.route::<Checkout>("checkouts"), |b| { b.include(checkout.transactional()); b.include(relay.workers_by_key(nonzero!(4))) .out_reply(to_bus); }) .with_broker(bus, |_b| {}) } src/main.rs use ruststream::memory::{MemoryBroker, MemoryPublish}; /// Each event goes out on the bus as it was written; the acknowledgement deletes its row. struct Relay; impl Handle<OrderPlaced, OrderPlaced> for Relay { fn handle( &self, event: &OrderPlaced, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<OrderPlaced, HandlerOutcome>> { ready(Ok(event.clone())) } } /// The service on the database `url` names. fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); // Nothing connects here: the broker builds its pool when the service starts. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, SqlitePoolOptions::new()); // The target broker is wrapped first, so its publish token exists before the scopes. let bus = MemoryBroker::new().bindable(); let to_bus = bus.bind(MemoryPublish); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("shop", "0.1.0")) // The table, created before the subscription checks it. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = SqliteConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker.route::<Checkout>("checkouts"), |b| { let checkout = subscriber("checkouts", PlaceOrder) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<Checkout>::new("checkouts")) .transactional(); b.include(checkout.build()); let relay = subscriber("order-events", Relay) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<OrderEvent>::new("order-events")) .workers_by_key(nonzero!(4)) .reply(); b.include(relay.build()).out_reply(to_bus); }) .with_broker(bus, |_b| {}) } relay reads order_events and answers each event with itself; the reply type names its destination, orders. The reply leaves through the bus: bindable() wraps the target broker, bind(MemoryPublish) mints a publish token for it, and .out_reply(to_bus) sends the replies of relay through that token. A Kafka or NATS service puts its own broker and publish policy in the same two lines. The reply is published before the event's row settles, and the acknowledgement deletes the row. The relay is at least once. A reply whose publish fails returns the event to the queue, and a crash after the publish and before the acknowledgement publishes it again. A consumer that must not act twice keeps the event's identity, the order here, and passes over one it has seen.

aggregate is the event's partition key, the order's id. workers_by_key(4) relays four orders at once and keeps the events of one order in the order they were written. That order holds within one relay subscription. A relay on several instances whose events must stay in order per aggregate across all of them keeps them in a FIFO group or in the advisory lock form. The relay needs no "sent" flag and no polling of its own: the claim is the queue's, the delay after a failed publish is a retry, and a cap with a dead-letter group parks an event the target keeps refusing. Tracking what you publish is the other shape: the outbox plugin records what a handler publishes and marks it once a consumer processed it, but its record commits on its own, outside the business transaction.

The tests in the example file publish checkouts through the harness and read what reached the bus with tb.broker::<MemoryBroker>().published(..). One order reaches the bus once, and its event row is gone. The same order checked out twice publishes one event: the second checkout fails, and its event rolled back. The event rows wake no subscription, so the tests run on the real clock with TestApp::start_live past the poll interval.

This guide retries a job now or later, caps its attempts and parks what keeps failing in a dead-letter group of the same table. A retry here is a statement on the job's row. The row keeps its id and its place in the table, counts one more attempt, and a delay is a time in one of its columns. Nothing lives only in the process: a job waiting for its retry survives a restart. The example is a mailer that sends emails through a provider.

src/main.rs const SCHEMA: &str = "CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS mail_jobs ( id INTEGER PRIMARY KEY, name TEXT NOT NULL, attempt INTEGER NOT NULL DEFAULT 1, retry_after TEXT NOT NULL DEFAULT (strftime('%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%f+00:00', 'now')), locked_until TEXT, payload BLOB NOT NULL )"; name is the group a row waits in: the subscription to emails reads the rows whose name is emails. attempt counts the deliveries of a row, the first one included. retry_after is the time a row becomes due; its default makes a new row due at once.

The provider refuses an email in three ways, and each needs a different outcome. Busy means its rate limit is spent: a retry right now would be refused again, so the email waits. Unavailable means it did not answer: retry tries again at once. Rejected means the mailbox does not exist, and another try gets the same answer, so the email is dropped. Macros Manual src/main.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::Connection; use sqlx::Sqlite; use sqlx::sqlite::SqlitePoolOptions; /// One row of `mail_jobs`; `name` is the queue the row waits in. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "mail_jobs")] struct SendMail { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(group)] name: String, #[field(attempt, generated)] attempt: i16, #[field(retry_after)] retry_after: DateTime<Utc>, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } /// How much longer each attempt waits after the provider said it was busy. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(1); #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<SendMail>::new("emails"))] async fn send(mail: &Mail, Ctx(attempt): Ctx<keys::Attempt>) -> HandlerOutcome { let attempt = attempt.unwrap_or(1); match deliver(mail, attempt).await { Ok(()) => HandlerOutcome::ack(), // The provider's rate limit is spent: a retry right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => { HandlerOutcome::retry_after(BACKOFF * u32::try_from(attempt).unwrap_or(u32::MAX)) } // The provider did not answer: the next attempt may reach it. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => HandlerOutcome::retry(), // The mailbox does not exist: every attempt gets the same answer. Err(Refusal::Rejected) => { tracing::warn!(to = %mail.to, "address rejected, dropped"); HandlerOutcome::drop() } } } src/main.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::Connection; use sqlx::Sqlite; use sqlx::sqlite::SqlitePoolOptions; /// One row of `mail_jobs`; `name` is the queue the row waits in. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct SendMail { id: i64, attempt: i16, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for SendMail { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<( Attempt, RetryAfter<DateTime<Utc>>, Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, Payload, )>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("mail_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .group(Column::new("name")) .attempt(Column::new("attempt").generated()) .retry_after(Column::new("retry_after")) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl AttemptRow for SendMail { type Attempt = i16; fn attempt(&self) -> &i16 { &self.attempt } } impl PayloadRow for SendMail { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } /// How much longer each attempt waits after the provider said it was busy. const BACKOFF: Duration = Duration::from_secs(1); struct Sender; impl Handle<Mail, (), (), InboxContext> for Sender { async fn handle( &self, mail: &Mail, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, InboxContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Ctx(attempt) = Ctx::<keys::Attempt>::from_context(ctx).await?; let attempt = attempt.unwrap_or(1); match deliver(mail, attempt).await { Ok(()) => Ok(()), // The provider's rate limit is spent: a retry right now would be refused again. Err(Refusal::Busy) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry_after( BACKOFF * u32::try_from(attempt).unwrap_or(u32::MAX), )), // The provider did not answer: the next attempt may reach it. Err(Refusal::Unavailable) => Err(HandlerOutcome::retry()), // The mailbox does not exist: every attempt gets the same answer. Err(Refusal::Rejected) => { tracing::warn!(to = %mail.to, "address rejected, dropped"); Err(HandlerOutcome::drop()) } } } } The handler owns the backoff. It reads the delivery's attempt and asks for a second more with each one: retry_after(d) writes "now" plus d into the row's retry_after, and no claim takes the row before then. A table without that column returns the row at once, and the runtime logs a warning. retry() returns the row to the queue at once; its next delivery reads one more attempt. drop() finishes the row as an acknowledgement does, so a rejected email leaves the table. A row whose payload does not decode spends its attempts like any other failure (Decoding).

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// The service on the database `url` names. fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); // Nothing connects here: the broker builds its pool when the service starts. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, SqlitePoolOptions::new()); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("mailer", "0.1.0")) // The table, created before the subscription checks it. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = SqliteConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker.route::<SendMail>("emails"), |b| { // Five deliveries, the first included; the fifth failure moves the row into the // `emails.dead` group. b.include(send) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("emails.dead"); b.include(review); }) } src/main.rs /// The service on the database `url` names. fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); // Nothing connects here: the broker builds its pool when the service starts. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, SqlitePoolOptions::new()); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("mailer", "0.1.0")) // The table, created before the subscription checks it. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = SqliteConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker.route::<SendMail>("emails"), |b| { // Five deliveries, the first included; the fifth failure moves the row into the // `emails.dead` group. let send = subscriber("emails", Sender).map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<SendMail>::new("emails")); b.include(send.build()) .max_attempts(nonzero!(5u32)) .dead_letter("emails.dead"); let review = subscriber("emails.dead", Review) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<SendMail>::new("emails.dead")); b.include(review.build()); }) } max_attempts reads the row's attempt. The fifth delivery that fails is not retried: dead_letter moves the row into the emails.dead group, payload and attempt as they were. A delayed retry counts against the cap as an immediate one does. The two steps come together: a mount that declares one without the other stops the service at startup. A table without a group column takes a table name in dead_letter instead, and the row moves into that table, which has the same columns.
documents.s: The cap and the dead-letter group

documents.t: The dead-letter group is an ordinary queue of the table, and review reads it like any other. Macros Manual src/main.rs #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<SendMail>::new("emails.dead"))] async fn review(mail: &Mail, Ctx(attempt): Ctx<keys::Attempt>) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::error!(to = %mail.to, ?attempt, "email not sent, needs a person"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } src/main.rs struct Review; impl Handle<Mail, (), (), InboxContext> for Review { async fn handle( &self, mail: &Mail, _outs: &(), ctx: &mut Context<'_, InboxContext>, ) -> Result<(), HandlerOutcome> { let Ctx(attempt) = Ctx::<keys::Attempt>::from_context(ctx).await?; tracing::error!(to = %mail.to, ?attempt, "email not sent, needs a person"); Ok(()) } } review logs the email for a person to look at and acknowledges it. A service that keeps its dead letters for an operator mounts no subscription on the group; the rows wait in the table. Sending them again is one statement of the service's own, which moves them back and resets their count: UPDATE mail_jobs SET name = 'emails', attempt = 1, locked_until = NULL WHERE name = 'emails.dead'; In a table with FIFO groups, retry() keeps a row at the head of its group, and retry_after(d) lets the rows due earlier pass it (Ordering).

The tests in the example file publish an email through the harness, as the service's own Publish writes it. A rejected address is dropped at once, which TestApp::start shows when the publish returns. An unanswered email and a busy provider need time to pass: the delayed row and the dead letter come back on the subscriptions' next poll. Those tests run on the real clock with TestApp::start_live, with a backoff of one second, and tb.advance waits it out. Testing a service on SQL covers the harness.

This guide runs a queue on several instances of a service and several workers in each, and sets how fast they see a new job. A queue table is shared by every instance that reads it. Nothing coordinates the instances but the database: each claims rows, and the form of the table keeps any row in one claim at a time. Two claimers never take the same row, in any form and on any database. The example renders invoices. The shop writes the invoice jobs with its own SQL, and the rendering service runs as many instances as the load asks for.

Macros Manual src/main.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::sqlite::SqlitePoolOptions; use sqlx::{Connection, Sqlite, SqliteConnection}; /// One row of `invoice_jobs`. #[derive(Inbox, sqlx::FromRow)] #[inbox(table = "invoice_jobs")] struct RenderInvoice { #[field(id, generated)] id: i64, #[field(locked_until)] locked_until: Option<DateTime<Utc>>, #[field(payload)] payload: Vec<u8>, } #[subscriber(InboxQueue::<RenderInvoice>::new("invoices"))] async fn render(invoice: &Invoice) -> HandlerOutcome { tracing::info!(invoice.number, "rendering"); HandlerOutcome::ack() } fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); // A row another program writes is seen within a quarter of a second. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, SqlitePoolOptions::new()) .poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(250)) .route::<RenderInvoice>("invoices"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoices", "0.1.0")) // The table, created before the subscription checks it. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = SqliteConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // Up to four invoices in work at once in this instance. b.include(render.workers(nonzero!(4))); }) } src/main.rs use ruststream_sqlx::prelude::*; use sqlx::sqlite::SqlitePoolOptions; use sqlx::{Connection, Sqlite, SqliteConnection}; /// One row of `invoice_jobs`. #[derive(sqlx::FromRow)] struct RenderInvoice { id: i64, payload: Vec<u8>, } impl InboxTable for RenderInvoice { type Id = i64; type Table = InboxSpec<(Lease<DateTime<Utc>>, Payload)>; const TABLE: Self::Table = InboxSpec::new("invoice_jobs", Column::new("id").generated()) .lease(Column::new("locked_until")) .payload(Column::new("payload")); fn id(&self) -> &i64 { &self.id } } impl PayloadRow for RenderInvoice { type Column = Vec<u8>; fn payload(&self) -> &[u8] { &self.payload } } struct Render; impl Handle<Invoice> for Render { fn handle( &self, invoice: &Invoice, _outs: &(), _ctx: &mut Context<'_>, ) -> impl Future<Output = Result<(), HandlerOutcome>> { tracing::info!(invoice.number, "rendering"); ready(Ok(())) } } fn service(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); // A row another program writes is seen within a quarter of a second. let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, SqlitePoolOptions::new()) .poll_interval(Duration::from_millis(250)) .route::<RenderInvoice>("invoices"); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoices", "0.1.0")) // The table, created before the subscription checks it. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = SqliteConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker, |b| { // Up to four invoices in work at once in this instance. let render = subscriber("invoices", Render) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<RenderInvoice>::new("invoices")) .workers(nonzero!(4)); b.include(render.build()); }) } workers(4) runs up to four invoices at once in each instance. The subscription keeps a claim in flight for each free worker, so its workers take rows at once instead of one after another. On SQLite, which takes one writer at a time, it keeps one claim in flight, and in the lease form that claim takes a row for every worker. A second instance on the same table adds four more workers, and no invoice goes to both.

A subscription claims while its claims come back full, so a backlog drains without a pause. After a claim that found fewer rows than it asked for, it waits the poll interval, one second unless set. Three things bound how long a new row waits: A publish through the broker wakes the subscriptions of its table in the same process at once, at the cost of one atomic operation per woken subscription. A row written by other means waits the poll interval: another program's insert, a trigger, an insert of the service, a publish from another instance. poll_interval(250 ms) here bounds that wait to a quarter of a second, at the price of four claim statements a second per subscription on an idle table. On Postgres, a notification ends the wait.
documents.s: How fast a new job is seen

documents.t: Macros Manual src/main.rs use sqlx::PgConnection; use sqlx::postgres::PgPoolOptions; /// The same service on Postgres: notifications wake it, and the poll each minute reaches a row /// whose notification was lost. fn service_on_postgres(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, PgPoolOptions::new()) .poll_interval(Duration::from_mins(1)) .listen_notify(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoices", "0.1.0")) // The table and its trigger, created before the subscription checks them. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = PgConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(POSTGRES_SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(ANNOUNCE).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker, |b| { b.include(render.workers(nonzero!(4))); }) } /// The trigger announces every row another program inserts: the channel is the table, and an /// empty payload wakes every subscription of it. const ANNOUNCE: &str = " CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION announce_invoice() RETURNS trigger AS $$ BEGIN PERFORM pg_notify(TG_TABLE_NAME, ''); RETURN NULL; END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql; CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER invoice_announced AFTER INSERT ON invoice_jobs FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION announce_invoice(); "; src/main.rs use sqlx::PgConnection; use sqlx::postgres::PgPoolOptions; /// The same service on Postgres: notifications wake it, and the poll each minute reaches a row /// whose notification was lost. fn service_on_postgres(url: &str) -> RustStream { let schema_url = url.to_owned(); let broker = SqlxBroker::from_url(url, PgPoolOptions::new()) .poll_interval(Duration::from_mins(1)) .listen_notify(); RustStream::new(AppInfo::new("invoices", "0.1.0")) // The table and its trigger, created before the subscription checks them. .on_startup(async move |()| { let mut conn = PgConnection::connect(&schema_url).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(POSTGRES_SCHEMA).execute(&mut conn).await?; sqlx::raw_sql(ANNOUNCE).execute(&mut conn).await?; conn.close().await }) .with_broker(broker, |b| { let render = subscriber("invoices", Render) .map_source(|_| InboxQueue::<RenderInvoice>::new("invoices")) .workers(nonzero!(4)); b.include(render.build()); }) } /// The trigger announces every row another program inserts: the channel is the table, and an /// empty payload wakes every subscription of it. const ANNOUNCE: &str = " CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION announce_invoice() RETURNS trigger AS $$ BEGIN PERFORM pg_notify(TG_TABLE_NAME, ''); RETURN NULL; END; $$ LANGUAGE plpgsql; CREATE OR REPLACE TRIGGER invoice_announced AFTER INSERT ON invoice_jobs FOR EACH ROW EXECUTE FUNCTION announce_invoice(); "; listen_notify() listens on one connection of the pool, and each subscription listens on its table's channel. Each publish of the broker runs pg_notify(channel, group) right after its write, so a subscription in another instance claims the row once it is visible. A writer outside RustStream sends the same notification itself; the trigger above does it for every insert, and its empty payload wakes every subscription of the table. With notifications the poll interval becomes a floor for what a notification missed, a minute here. Notifications have a price, and the switch is off unless set. The broker keeps one connection of the pool for its whole life. Each publish runs one more statement. A transaction that notifies takes a lock global to the server at commit, so commits of notifying transactions run one after another; a service with many concurrent writers measures that before it turns notifications on (NOTIFY).

A subscription never holds more than the pool's size less one connection, so the pool always keeps one for the handlers, their publishes and the settlements. A pool too small for its workers runs fewer deliveries at once; it does not fail. In the lease form a pool of n + 1 lets every free worker of workers(n) claim at once; the row lock and advisory lock forms also hold a connection for each job in work (Connections). Running in production sizes the pool for a whole service.

Each instance reads "now" from its host's clock to claim, delay and lease rows (Time). The hosts that serve one table keep their clocks in step, well within a lease, as NTP does. Where they cannot, a table on DatabaseClock reads the database's clock in every statement; the lease form keeps the host's clock, so such a table takes the row lock or the advisory lock form.

The tests in the example file run the service on SQLite in memory. Two instances, each with a pool of its own, start on one table that holds twenty invoices, and between them render each invoice once. A row another program writes is seen within the quarter second of the poll interval. A publish through the broker reaches its own instance at once. Those rows wake no subscription, so the tests that wait for them run on the real clock with TestApp::start_live. A last test runs the Postgres service against a database of its own and finds an insert claimed long before the minute's poll; it reads the server's address from POSTGRES_TEST_URL and skips without it.

A test runs the service's own app with TestApp against a real database: SQLite in memory, or a database of the test's own on a server. A queue's behaviour lives in its SQL: the claim, the settlement, the service's own Publish. So the harness has no model of a database. Its in-process mode runs the service's statements against the database the test hands the service, and keeps the books the harness waits on. The service under test makes thumbnails. A small image is made at once. The resizer takes a large image only on a second try, so the first delivery of a large image is put off for a minute with retry_after. The app is built by service(url), so a test chooses the database and main uses the production one. The tests need the testing feature of ruststream-sqlx in [dev-dependencies].

Macros Manual src/main.rs /// A database in memory that every connection naming it shares, alive while one of them is /// open: the test holds that one beside the pool it reads the table through. The service /// creates the table when it starts. async fn database( name: &str, ) -> Result<(String, SqlitePool, SqliteConnection), Box<dyn Error>> { let url = format!("sqlite:file:{name}?mode=memory&cache=shared"); let options: SqliteConnectOptions = url.parse()?; let keeper = SqliteConnection::connect_with(&options).await?; let pool = SqlitePoolOptions::new() .min_connections(1) .idle_timeout(None) .connect_with(options) .await?; Ok((url, pool, keeper)) } /// The scenario, on whichever database the app runs. async fn a_small_image_is_made_at_once(broker: BrokerHandle<'_>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let image = Image { path: "cat.png".to_owned(), large: false, }; broker.message(&image).publish().await?; broker .subscriber("thumbnails") .assert_called_once() .with(&image) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); Ok(()) } #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn in_process() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let (url, pool, _keeper) = database("guide_testing").await?; let tb = TestApp::start(service(&url)).await?; a_small_image_is_made_at_once(tb.broker::<SqlxBroker<Sqlite>>()).await?; let left: i64 = sqlx::query_scalar("SELECT count(*) FROM thumbnail_jobs") .fetch_one(&pool) .await?; assert_eq!(left, 0, "the acknowledgement deleted the row"); Ok(()) } src/main.rs /// A database in memory that every connection naming it shares, alive while one of them is /// open: the test holds that one beside the pool it reads the table through. The service /// creates the table when it starts. async fn database( name: &str, ) -> Result<(String, SqlitePool, SqliteConnection), Box<dyn Error>> { let url = format!("sqlite:file:{name}?mode=memory&cache=shared"); let options: SqliteConnectOptions = url.parse()?; let keeper = SqliteConnection::connect_with(&options).await?; let pool = SqlitePoolOptions::new() .min_connections(1) .idle_timeout(None) .connect_with(options) .await?; Ok((url, pool, keeper)) } /// The scenario, on whichever database the app runs. async fn a_small_image_is_made_at_once(broker: BrokerHandle<'_>) -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let image = Image { path: "cat.png".to_owned(), large: false, }; broker.message(&image).publish().await?; broker .subscriber("thumbnails") .assert_called_once() .with(&image) .settled(HandlerOutcome::ack()); Ok(()) } #[tokio::test(flavor = "multi_thread", worker_threads = 2)] async fn in_process() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let (url, pool, _keeper) = database("manual_guide_testing").await?; let tb = TestApp::start(service(&url)).await?; a_small_image_is_made_at_once(tb.broker::<SqlxBroker<Sqlite>>()).await?; let left: i64 = sqlx::query_scalar("SELECT count(*) FROM thumbnail_jobs") .fetch_one(&pool) .await?; assert_eq!(left, 0, "the acknowledgement deleted the row"); Ok(()) } database creates a SQLite database in memory that every connection naming it shares. It lives while one of those connections is open, so the test holds one beside the pool it reads the table through. The service creates the table when it starts, as in production. TestApp::start connects the production app to it in process, and the test addresses the broker by its production type, tb.broker::<SqlxBroker<Sqlite>>(). The image goes in through the route and the service's own Publish, as in production. publish returns once the handler it woke has settled, so the lines after it read finished state: how thumbnail settled the row, and what the test's own query finds in the table. A row written with the service's own SQL before the app starts, a seed or a migration, is counted when its subscription opens, so settle waits for it as for a published message. A row written that way while the test runs is counted only once a claim takes it, so settle does not wait for it; such a test runs on the real clock and lets the poll interval pass, as Enqueueing jobs does. The scenario takes the broker's handle as an argument, so the Postgres test below runs it too. A table without a payload column hands its handler the row itself (Rows). A test of such a handler checks the row with with_value and received_values in place of with and received.

Macros Manual src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_large_image_is_made_a_minute_later() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let (url, _pool, _keeper) = database("guide_testing_clock").await?; // The queue reads "now" from this clock, and the database calls run off it. A paused // clock takes the single-threaded runtime `#[tokio::test]` starts. tokio::time::pause(); let tb = TestApp::start(service(&url)).await?; tb.broker::<SqlxBroker<Sqlite>>() .message(&Image { path: "panorama.png".to_owned(), large: true, }) .publish() .await?; tb.advance(Duration::from_secs(61)).await?; // Put off for a minute, then made. let outcomes = tb .broker::<SqlxBroker<Sqlite>>() .subscriber("thumbnails") .assert_called(2) .outcomes(); assert_eq!(outcomes, [Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Ack]); Ok(()) } src/main.rs #[tokio::test] async fn a_large_image_is_made_a_minute_later() -> Result<(), Box<dyn Error>> { let (url, _pool, _keeper) = database("manual_guide_testing_clock").await?; // The queue reads "now" from this clock, and the database calls run off it. A paused // clock takes the single-threaded runtime `#[tokio::test]` starts. tokio::time::pause(); let tb = TestApp::start(service(&url)).await?; tb.broker::<SqlxBroker<Sqlite>>() .message(&Image { path: "panorama.png".to_owned(), large: true, }) .publish() .await?; tb.advance(Duration::from_secs(61)).await?; // Put off for a minute, then made. let outcomes = tb .broker::<SqlxBroker<Sqlite>>() .subscriber("thumbnails") .assert_called(2) .outcomes(); assert_eq!(outcomes, [Outcome::Nack, Outcome::Ack]); Ok(()) } In process the queue reads "now" from the tokio clock, anchored to the system clock when the broker connected. The test pauses that clock, and advance moves it: the large image's row comes due a minute later, and the second delivery makes the thumbnail. The minute costs nothing. The database calls run off the paused clock, so it does not jump while the database answers. A lease runs out the same way when the clock passes it. A table on the database's clock reads the database's time, which the test clock does not move, and a clock of the service's own stays in force; tests of those run on the real clock.
